articles.title: 1300 BC: Miners worked a copper vein in Spain with hundreds of stone hammers; more than 3,000 years later, researchers found chemical matches in 11 Scandinavian bronze objects, hinting at a far-reaching trade network
articles.summary: A mine in south-western Spain is offering new clues about how copper travelled across Bronze Age Europe, potentially linking miners in the Iberian
articles.body: A mine in south-western Spain is offering new clues about how copper travelled across Bronze Age Europe, potentially linking miners in the Iberian Peninsula with communities in Scandinavia thousands of kilometres away. Around 1300 BC, people were extracting copper ore at Las Minillas, using stone tools to work deposits deep underground. Centuries later, bronze objects found in Scandinavia would preserve chemical signatures consistent with the metals produced at this Spanish site, offering evidence of connections that may have crossed much of Europe.A study published on October 26, 2026, in the archaeological journal Antiquity, published by Cambridge University Press, examines the mining evidence and compares the site's ores and metal remains with more than 300 Late Bronze Age bronze objects from Scandinavia. Researchers identified 11 objects whose chemical composition and lead isotope ratios were consistent with Las Minillas. The findings suggest that southern Iberia may have played a more important role in Europe's prehistoric copper supply than previously recognised, although the precise routes and mechanisms of exchange remain uncertain.A major Bronze Age mining site emerges in SpainLas Minillas is located near Granja de Torrehermosa in Badajoz, Extremadura, in south-western Spain. Although the Iberian Peninsula contains extensive copper deposits, the scale and chronology of prehistoric mining in the region have not been as thoroughly established as those of some other European mining districts. Fieldwork at Las Minillas, carried out since 2020, has changed that picture. Excavations in 2021 and 2023, supported by surface surveys, geophysical investigations and drilling, revealed extensive mining workings, areas used for habitation and evidence of metal production.Radiocarbon dating indicates that copper extraction took place at the site from approximately 1350 to 750 BC, covering much of the Late Bronze Age. The researchers identified mining trenches that followed the copper-bearing vein, reaching depths of 8.2 metres and widths of between two and four metres. The team documented 892 stone tools, including 735 grooved stone hammers associated with mining. Charcoal deposits also suggest that miners used fire-setting, a technique in which rock is heated to make it easier to fracture. Copper droplets, slag and a possible furnace provide evidence of smelting at the site. Together, these findings make Las Minillas the largest securely dated Late Bronze Age copper mine excavated in Iberia to date.Chemical evidence connects Spain with Scandinavian bronzeTo investigate where copper from Las Minillas might have travelled, the researchers analysed lead isotope ratios and trace elements in samples from the mine, including ores, slags and metal droplets. Lead isotope analysis can help archaeologists compare metal objects with geological deposits because different ore sources can have distinctive isotopic signatures. Researchers also examine elements such as silver, antimony and nickel to assess whether objects share compositional characteristics with particular mining areas.The team compared the Las Minillas results with data from more than 300 Late Bronze Age bronze objects discovered at sites across Scandinavia. Eleven objects, representing different artefact types, showed isotope ratios and chemical compositions consistent with the Spanish mining material. The comparison was not based on a single measurement. Similar ranges of silver and antimony concentrations strengthened the association, while nickel levels in the Scandinavian objects overlapped with some, though not all, of the samples from Las Minillas.The dates of the objects also offer useful context. Seven were assigned to Period V of the Nordic Bronze Age, approximately 900-700 BC, which overlaps with the latest documented phase of mining at Las Minillas. Two others belonged to Period VI, approximately 700-500 BC, and therefore post-dated the mine's final documented exploitation.Southern Iberia may have supplied a wider European networkThe findings have implications beyond a single mine. Before this research, copper supplies from regions such as the Austrian Alps and Wales were known to have reached communities across northern Europe, including Scandinavia. However, production at some major mining districts, including Great Orme in Wales and Mitterberg in Austria, declined around the transition from the Middle to the Late Bronze Age. The researchers suggest that southern Iberia may have become a more important source as these established production centres waned.Las Minillas was not an isolated operation. Archaeological surveys have identified dozens of potential prehistoric mining sites across south-western Iberia, although many still require more precise dating to establish whether they were active during the Late Bronze Age. The study proposes that these sites may have formed part of a broader Southern Iberian Copper Mining Complex. Estimates of copper output at Las Minillas range from a minimum of 49 tonnes to a cautious estimate of 197 tonnes and an optimistic estimate of 738 tonnes, illustrating both the potential scale of production and the uncertainty surrounding its reconstruction.A trade connection, not yet a complete route mapThe chemical matches do not establish exactly how the copper reached Scandinavia. The metal may have passed through several communities and trading centres before being fashioned into bronze objects, and the researchers cannot identify a single route from the evidence currently available. Further dating, excavations and chemical analyses will be needed to determine how many other Iberian mines contributed to European metal supplies and how these networks operated.Nevertheless, the research adds southern Spain to the discussion of major Bronze Age copper-producing regions. The stone hammers, deep mining trenches and chemical signatures preserved at Las Minillas suggest that communities in Iberia were connected to a much wider world of metal production and exchange than the surviving archaeological evidence once indicated.

articles.title: In the 1960s, scientists studying the venom of a Brazilian pit viper found a compound that lowered blood pressure, and it led to captopril, one of the first widely used blood pressure pills, approved in the US in 1981
articles.summary: Long before modern medical science emerged, nature held answers to healing, protection and healthy living within its bounds.
articles.body: Long before modern medical science emerged, nature held answers to healing, protection and healthy living within its bounds. Across several communities and spiritual cosmologies, the natural world has been viewed as the guide for the human world, as have the species that reside in it. Among the myriad spcies that have been a major subject of scientifc study, the animal venom has held serious importance. Therefore, native to parts of South American, including Brazil, a pit viper that possesses harmful venom was researched in the 1960s. The snake in question was Bothrops jararaca, commonly known as the Brazilian lancehead or jararaca.As researchers investigated its biolgical effects, they discovered compounds that would help shape the evolution of a new class of medicine, soemthing that would go on to change the use of western drugs in cardiovascular medicine, as this pit viper went on to change the treatment of blood pressure. With this seminal discovery, a research led a new pathway for a harmful substance to become a paramount drug. This work contributd to the development of captopril, an oral drug approved in the United states in 1981 for treating hypertension.The discovery hidden in snake venomThe research began sometime in the year 1965 with a young Brazilian pharmacologist, Sergio Ferreira, who published a paper, that was based on his PhD thesis, in the British Journal of Pharmacology . He described the properties of an extract of snake venom where he desrcibred the potential properties, of a snake venom and indetified a substance that enhanced the effects of bradykinin, a naturally occuring peptide that involved in wideing blood vessels and subsequently lowering blood pressure.Further investigation revealed that the venom contained small molecules called bradykinin-potentiating peptides. These findings became particularly important as scientists established how the peptides interacted with the body's blood-pressure-regulating systems. One enzyme that recieved considerable attention: angiotensin-converting enzyme, commonly known as ACE. Under normal circumstances, ACE helps convert angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a substance that constricts blood vessels and contributes to an increase in blood pressure. The enzyme also breaks down bradykinin, which helps blood vessels relax.From venom peptide to a medicineUnderstanding the biological effects of the venom was only the beginning. The challenge was to turn those findings into a medicine that patients could take reliably. Researchers discovered that the venom-derived peptide teprotide could inhibit ACE and lower blood pressure. However, teprotide could not be administered orally, making it less practical for routine treatment. Scientists needed a different compound that could reproduce the desired effect while being suitable for use as a tablet. Captopril became the first ACE inhibitor approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration in 1981. Its development marked an important milestone in pharmacology, demonstrating how observations made in nature could guide the design of medicines for human use.Why this discovery still mattersHigh blood pressure, or hypertension, can place sustained strain on the heart and blood vessels, increasing the risk of serious cardiovascular complications. Because the condition may develop without obvious symptoms, treatment often depends on identifying elevated blood pressure and managing it over time.Captopril has offered new ways of responding to this problem by targeting the biological processes that are involved in regulating blood pressure. It became a vital medicine in the treatment of hypertension, and ACE inhibitors subsequently developed into an established class of cardiovascular drugs. These medicines are also used in other clinical settings, including certain cases of heart failure and kidney disease, depending on the individual patient's condition.However, the research on snake venom doesnt propogate the use of snake venom itself as a replacement of a prescribed drug. While, the venom has been able to rpovide researches with a biological clue, the years of researhc, experiemntation and development has enabled the drug to be established for use today.From a Brazilian pit viper to a laboratory designed pill, the journey of captopril has been long. However, the 15-20 years spent between the research and the drug's approval saw the field of medical science evolve. Today, decades later, multiple researchers around the world attest to how the natural world has opened many doors for discovery that would have otherwise remained out of reach.

articles.title: In 1901, sponge divers off the Greek island of Antikythera recovered a corroded lump of bronze from a 2,000-year-old shipwreck; scans later showed it was a geared device built to predict eclipses
articles.summary: \"Astronomy compels the soul to look upwards and leads us from this world to another,\" said Plato.
articles.body: "Astronomy compels the soul to look upwards and leads us from this world to another," said Plato. But even as the skies above us have changed over centuries, the stars have continued to hold the same fascination for those seeking to understand the universe.There are some discoveries that do not immediately reveal to us the extent of what they hold within them, lying quietly beneath layers of dust and corrosion until someone curious enough comes along and happens look a little closer.The discovery of the Antikythera Mechanism is one such story where a seemingly unostentatious piece of corroded bronze was recovered from the depths of the Mediterranean, revealing an extraordinary knowledge of astronomy and mechanical engineering that had existed more than 2,000 years ago.What appeared to be a little more than a lump of metal was, in fact, later revealed to be an elaborate astronomical calculator, built by the ancient greeks to follow the movements of celestial bodies and predict events in the skies.It was in 1990, when a group of Greek sponge divers discovered an ancient shipwreck off the coast of Antikythera, an island situated between Crete and Peloponnese. The divers who were exploring the seabed came across the remains fo a large cargo vessel,whre pottery, glassware, statues and other antique objects lay scattered. Looking at this, recovery operations followed from 1901 to well into 1920, with several artefacts eventuaslly being brought to the National Archaeolgical Museum in Athens.An unexpected discoveryAmong these copious objects gathered, there was also a heavily corroded mass of bronze, which at first gathered verey little interest of researchers. However, it was only in 1902, that when archaeolgists examined the object more closely, that this small toothedgear became prominet.The object came to be known as the Antikythera Mechanism, named after the island near which it was discovered. Although its original appearance has been obscured by centuries underwater, researchers have been able to reconstruct much of its internal arrangement through modern imaging technologies.In a 2006 study published in Nature, researchers, including Tony Freeth and his colleagues, used high-resolution X-ray tomography and surface imaging to examine the surviving fragments, revealing a sophisticated arrangement of interlocking bronze gears. The study established that the mechanism was capable of calculating astronomical cycles, including the movements of the Sun and Moon, while also predicting solar and lunar eclipses.Why was the gear used 2,000 years agoWhat makes the discovery particularly remarkable is the complexity hidden within its construction. The mechanism contained at least 30 bronze gear wheels, arranged in a system that allowed the movement of one component to correspond with the changing positions of celestial bodies. Rather than simply marking the passage of days or months, it could represent the relationship between different astronomical cycles.Apart from its astronomical calculations, the mechanism also carried a connection to the cultural life of ancient Greece. Its calendar included an Olympiad-related display, marking the four-year cycle associated with the ancient Greek athletic competitions. This is particularly interesting because it suggests that the device was not limited to observing celestial movements, but brought together astronomy, the measurement of time and the organisation of important cultural events. The same instrument that could calculate lunar cycles and predict eclipses could also help place human activities within a wider understanding of time.There is also evidence that the mechanism may have displayed the positions of planets, although much of this part of its construction has not survived. In a 2018 review published in Nature Astronomy, researchers John H. Seiradakis and Mike Edmunds examined the accumulated findings and discussed how the inscriptions on the surviving fragments support the possibility of planetary displays. The researchers also highlighted the uncertainties that continue to surround its origins, construction and intended purpose.Why the calculator has more questions to answerDespite the extraordinary amount of research carried out on the Antikythera Mechanism, several questions remain unanswered. Its exact maker is unknown, as is the identity of the person or group for whom it was constructed. The shipwreck itself is generally dated to the first century BC, while the mechanism is believed to have been manufactured earlier, around the second century BC. How such an intricate scientific instrument came to be part of the vessel's cargo, and where it was originally intended to travel, remains uncertain. Its discovery also raises questions about how much of ancient mechanical knowledge has been lost, particularly since no surviving device of comparable complexity appears in the historical record for many centuries afterwards.Today, the Antikythera Mechanism stands as one of the most extraordinary surviving examples of ancient Greek scientific ingenuity. Its fragments may be incomplete, its original purpose may never be fully established, who created it may never be known, but the calculations preserved within its corroded gears continue to reveal an entire civilisation that was keenly looking up at the skies with remarkable, unmoving precision.

articles.title: In 2003, archaeologists in London found a sealed tin pot nearly 2,000 years old still full of a Roman face cream, with the finger marks of the last person to scoop out the white paste still visible inside
articles.summary: The length and breadth of beauty preserved across time, from one era to another, tell stories that continue to unfold.
articles.body: The length and breadth of beauty preserved across time, from one era to another, tell stories that continue to unfold. In the world around us, multiple time zones and realities coalesce, with people across different periods finding their own ways of preserving and enhancing their appearance. Some beauty secrets still lie buried in the world around us, remnants of centuries gone by, while certain marks of beauty lie indelibly etched, sealed, and buried beneath the passage of time. In 2003, a rather unusual discovery beneath the streets of London offered something far more personal: a small tin container, almost 2,000 years old, still holding the remnants of a cosmetic cream, complete with the fingerprints of the person who had last used it.In July 2003, archaeologists excavating a Roman temple complex at Tabard Square in Southwark, London, came across a sealed metal pot, o that would soon become one of the more fascinating discoveries in the study of ancient cosmetics. Measuring approximately 6 centimetres in diameter, the little container had remained remarkably well preserved, with its close-fitting lid protecting the white paste inside. When conservators at the London museum finally opened it, they found not only the ancient substance but also the delicate impressions of fingers left behind by someone who had scooped out the cream almost two millennia earlier.A Roman beauty ritual preserved through centuriesThe discovery initially left archaeologists with several questions about what the substance might have been used for. Its white appearance and peculiar smell prompted researchers to ascertain whether it was a medicinal ointment, a cosmetic preparation or even something associated with religious ceremonies. The container had been recovered from a ditch surrounding the temple complex, which was believed to have held ritual significance.The archaeological site itself was an important Roman religious centre, with two Romano-Celtic temples and a possible guesthouse among its discoveries, dating to approximately the middle of the 2nd century AD. The little tin pot, therefore, was not simply an isolated household object but part of a much wider archaeological picture of religious and everyday life in Roman London.However, it was the contents of the container that offered scientists an opportunity to look beyond the circumstances of its discovery.In 2004, researchers from the University of Bristol published their findings in the scientific journal Nature, following a detailed chemical examination of the ancient cream. Their investigation revealed that the white paste was most likely a cosmetic preparation, with a formulation surprisingly reminiscent of some of the basic principles behind modern moisturising creams and foundations.What went into a Roman face cream?The chemical analysis identified three principal ingredients: animal fat, starch and tin oxide. The animal fat, which researchers believed probably came from a cow or goat, and starch each accounted for approximately 40 per cent of the cream. The remaining ingredient was tin oxide, which gave the otherwise pale preparation its distinctive white appearance.What makes this formulation particularly interesting is that each ingredient seems to have served a different purpose. The animal fat, presumably belonging to a sheep or cow, may have provided the cream with its moisturising base, while the starch helped reduce the greasy sensation that would otherwise have been felt after applying the animal fat. Interestingly, starch continues to be used in certain modern body lotions and hand creams for a similar purpose.White face preparations in the Roman world could contain lead compounds, including lead acetate, which presented considerable health risks. Tin oxide offered a different way of achieving a white pigment. Researchers considered its use in the London cream significant, although the discovery alone does not establish whether its maker deliberately chose it as a safer alternative.Bringing an ancient beauty secret back to lifePerhaps the most fascinating aspect of the research was that scientists did not stop at identifying the ingredients. Through these chemical findings, the team led by Richard Evershed at the University of Bristol recreated the cream with fresh materials, allowing them to examine how the original formulation might have felt and appeared when applied to the skin.The reconstructed preparation produced a smooth, white cream with a powdery texture, offering coverage comparable to some modern foundation products. The researchers found that the starch helped give the mixture its softer finish, while the tin oxide provided the characteristic pale appearance.Even years later, this discovery remains a compelling archaeological find. Through the quotidian object it draws a connection to a world not known before. Alongside the science that went into making this cream, the intimate human connection has survived too, belonging to a person whose name, appearance, story may never be known.

articles.title: In 2022, an 800-gram pink rock was found in the Sahara Desert; NASA-funded researchers have now confirmed it came from Mars more than 4.1 billion years ago and preserves signs of the planet's ancient water
articles.summary: A rock that spent more than four billion years preserving clues about Mars' early history was found lying in the Sahara Desert, looking like an ordinary
articles.body: A rock that spent more than four billion years preserving clues about Mars' early history was found lying in the Sahara Desert, looking like an ordinary pink stone. Discovered in 2022, the 800-gram rock has since turned out to be one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever identified on Earth. Its mineral composition contains evidence of ancient volcanic activity and interactions between water and rock, offering scientists a rare opportunity to study what Mars was like billions of years before it became the cold, dry planet we know today.In a NASA report published on October 29, 2026, the agency detailed findings from a NASA-funded study of the meteorite, named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered. According to the primary source, NASA-funded researchers, including scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, determined that the rock formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. The findings, published in the journal Science, provide a new look at the formation of the Martian crust and the role water played in shaping the planet's early surface.How a pink rock from the Sahara turned out to be MartianWhen Teghaza 001 was discovered, researchers did not immediately know its age or exact origin. Scientists at the University of New Mexico had already identified it as a Martian meteorite by examining its oxygen isotopes. These isotopes act like geochemical fingerprints, helping researchers distinguish rocks from different planetary bodies. However, the meteorite's unusual texture and mineral composition caught the attention of Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. Although Martian meteorites had been studied before, this specimen contained minerals and structures that made it particularly interesting.The rock is now considered one of roughly 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth and among the three oldest known examples. Its importance lies in the variety of minerals it contains, which provide a more complete record of the planet's early geological history.What its minerals reveal about ancient MarsResearchers found that Teghaza 001 contains a mixture of igneous minerals, which form when molten rock cools and solidifies. These minerals offer clues about how the Martian crust developed from magma. The rock also contains zircon crystals, which are particularly valuable to geologists because they preserve information about the conditions and timing of a rock's formation. By studying these crystals and other mineral grains, scientists could establish the meteorite's age and identify later changes caused by water.The team used an in-situ rubidium-strontium dating technique developed with contributions from researchers at the California Institute of Technology. Unlike traditional methods that require dissolving an entire sample, this technique examines individual mineral grains. The researchers needed only a piece smaller than a fingernail, allowing them to preserve most of the rare meteorite for future investigations. The analysis revealed that the rock had been altered by water around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting that its original formation occurred even earlier.Evidence of water on the Red PlanetOne of the most significant aspects of the discovery is what it reveals about water on early Mars. The mineral chemistry, oxygen isotopes and textures suggest that water interacted with the planet's crust during its early geological history. A separate study published in Science Advances in June 2026 examined the meteorite's water content, providing further information about how water influenced the Martian surface.Lee Saper, a co-author of the research who conducted the work as a postdoctoral scholar at JPL, said the meteorite offered a rare sample of Martian crust from a region not previously represented in the collection of meteorites studied on Earth. He explained that it records interactions between water and rock and may even preserve traces of the Martian atmosphere from a period when the planet was losing water. These findings point towards a more dynamic water cycle on early Mars than scientists could previously reconstruct from many available meteorite samples.Scientists still do not know its exact birthplaceAlthough researchers have confirmed that Teghaza 001 came from Mars, identifying its precise birthplace remains difficult. The team compared its mineral composition and chemistry with observations made by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and identified 13 possible locations on the planet that could match the meteorite.The rock's characteristics are particularly similar to materials observed in Mars' cratered southern highlands. However, scientists cannot yet establish which specific location produced it. Like other Martian meteorites, Teghaza 001 was thrown into space by a powerful impact on the planet's surface before eventually travelling through space and reaching Earth.Researchers believe the meteorite could help answer questions about how the Martian crust formed, how water interacted with rocks and how the planet's environment changed over billions of years. With further studies planned, scientists hope the unusual pink rock will provide more clues about Mars' ancient past.

articles.title: Cornell scientists engineered tomatoes that turn red-purple when nitrogen is low and are testing whether the colour change can help farmers use fertiliser more precisely
articles.summary: Cornell University scientists have developed genetically engineered tomato plants that turn red-purple when nitrogen becomes scarce, giving farmers a
articles.body: Cornell University scientists have developed genetically engineered tomato plants that turn red-purple when nitrogen becomes scarce, giving farmers a visible warning that crops may need fertiliser. Called RedAlert, the plants have moved beyond greenhouse experiments and are being tested under real-world conditions at Cornell’s Musgrave Research Farm in Aurora, New York. Visitors saw the experiment on July 30 during the 2026 Aurora Farm Field Day, which showcased agricultural research. According to a September report in the Cornell Chronicle, the plants produce betanin, the red-purple pigment found in beets, when deprived of nitrogen. Researchers hope these living sensors could help growers identify nutrient shortages sooner and apply fertiliser more precisely. The plants are not intended to enter the food supply. Instead, they could eventually be planted alongside conventional crops to monitor nitrogen availability in a field.RedAlert tomatoes: how nitrogen deficiency triggers a red-purple colour changeThe project is part of Cornell’s Centre for Research on Programmable Plant Systems (CROPPS), which investigates ways to engineer plants to communicate information about their surroundings. Plant scientist Margaret Frank first conceived the idea behind the colour-changing tomatoes. Initial work on the nitrogen-sensing system involved researchers Brandon Williams and Yinan Wu, while doctoral students Jacob Belding and Ava Forystek developed the RedAlert Living Sensors. Their invention won the Graduate Runner-Up award at the 2025 Collegiate Inventors Competition, receiving $5,000, according to the National Inventors Hall of Fame. RedAlert uses a biological signalling pathway through which plants detect nitrogen availability around their roots and transmit information to their shoots. The engineered plants respond by producing betanin, making nitrogen stress visible through a change in colour.Nitrogen-deficient plants can develop yellowing leaves, but RedAlert is designed to offer a different visual signal that researchers hope could help growers recognise nutrient shortages earlier. In its 2025 report on the invention, the Cornell Chronicle reported that shades of redness reflect varying gradients of available soil nitrogen. However, the researchers are still analysing field data to establish how reliably colour intensity corresponds to nitrogen concentration under real growing conditions. The potential agricultural benefit is reducing unnecessary fertiliser use. Cornell’s 2025 report noted that farmers can apply up to 50% more nitrogen than needed. Excess nitrogen can run off into groundwater and lakes, contributing to harmful algal blooms. A visible biological sensor could help growers identify where fertilizer is needed instead of relying solely on soil measurements that may not capture differences across an entire field.Cornell’s 2026 field trial tests RedAlert under real growing conditionsThe 2026 experiment at Musgrave Research Farm marks the project’s second field season at the site. During the first season in 2025, researchers planted the sensor tomatoes among corn. The plants distinguished low-nitrogen conditions from conditions with sufficient nitrogen. A secondary experiment aimed at using the tomatoes to predict corn yields proved more difficult because the two crops require different management practices. For the 2026 season, researchers established a separate plot containing RedAlert plants alongside non-engineered tomatoes. The experimental plants received 3 nitrogen treatments: a low dose, a standard dose and a recovery treatment that began with low nitrogen before receiving a standard amount.The season presented challenges. Powdery mildew and hot conditions early in the growing period made measuring plant characteristics more difficult. Nevertheless, researchers observed recovery in plants that had experienced early nitrogen stress. Green leaves emerged after nitrogen was added to mature plants, particularly in a new line being tested. Doctoral student Sam Mosher, who is leading the field trials, highlighted the importance of observing recovery in mature plants, which greenhouse experiments rarely grow to that stage. Researchers are analysing soil and leaf samples to investigate whether nitrogen levels explain the observed colour differences.They are also using low-flying drones and handheld spectrophotometers to measure plant colour systematically. The 2026 Cornell Chronicle report noted that visitors asked whether the intensity of the purple-red colour reliably matches nitrogen concentration. Mosher said that if nitrogen proves to be the driver of local colour changes, the new line would be a promising sensor candidate. The field data are still being analysed, so the relationship requires further verification.Can nitrogen-sensing tomatoes help farmers reduce fertiliser waste?Researchers hope sentinel plants could provide a more continuous picture of nitrogen availability across agricultural fields. Unlike occasional soil tests, living sensors could potentially reveal changes as plants grow, helping farmers decide when additional fertiliser is necessary. However, practical questions remain unresolved, including how many sentinel plants a field would require and how growers should interpret their colour changes. Visitors at the 2026 field day also raised questions about consumer acceptance and whether the technology could detect other stresses, such as phosphorus deficiency or water shortages. Cornell’s report described these questions as issues that researchers still need to address.RedAlert remains an experimental technology, not a commercially established fertiliser-monitoring system. Its future usefulness will depend on whether further field trials can reliably connect visible colour changes with nitrogen availability under varying growing conditions. For now, the researchers are working to establish that relationship and determine how the plants might fit into practical farm management.

articles.title: SpaceX Hits Back at T-Mobile’s ‘Misplaced Desire’ to Harm Starlink by Opposing ‘Modernized’ Spectrum Rules
articles.summary: Billionaire Elon Musk-led Space Exploration Technologies Corp. slammed legacy telecom operators like T-Mobile US Inc. in a letter to the Federal Communicatio...
articles.body:
Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Billionaire Elon Musk -led Space Exploration Technologies Corp. slammed legacy telecom operators like T-Mobile US Inc. in a letter to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over the agency's proposed spectrum rule changes.

In the letter dated October 28, SpaceX said that the agency should reject the "technically unsound recommendations from the Aerospace and Flight Test Radio Coordinating Council (AFTRCC) and T-Mobile," which want power limits on satellite transmissions, saying the signals could interfere with flight telemetry tracking systems.

"Unfortunately, the misplaced desire to harm a competitor has led many incumbents to oppose modernized rules that would bring direct-to-cell service to underserved border communities," SpaceX said.

"AFTRCC is now purely a lobbying organization whose mission is to protect legacy companies and their comments should not be viewed as independent or objective," SpaceX alleged in the letter.

SpaceX also slammed T-Mobile's base station protection demands, which, the commercial space flight giant says, would create 250-mile-wide buffer zones around cell towers, which would lead to "disenfranchising millions from direct-to- cell service in the countries where the limit is applied."

SpaceX urged the FCC to reject the base station protection plea from T-Mobile. SpaceX also said that the cell tower antennas were directional and therefore "inherently more resilient to interference" from satellite signals and transmissions. "The Commission should not adopt T-Mobile's proposed limits for base-station protection," SpaceX said in the letter.

Earlier this month, Musk had predicted that the telecom industry was about to experience an "earthquake" after SpaceX acquired 800 MHz spectrum.

The letter comes as Verizon Communications Inc. CEO Dan Schulman , during the telecom operator's recent Q3 2026 earnings call, said that SpaceX would have to spend $500 billion to compete with traditional cellular service providers.

Other telecom company executives have also been skeptical of SpaceX's cellular service, which would rely on femtocells, which are small cellular base stations that improve connectivity.

articles.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward | TechCrunch
articles.summary: An NAACP lawsuit accuses the SpaceX-owned AI company of violating the Clean Air Act.
articles.body:
A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis.

Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.

xAI sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, claiming that the turbines are exempt from permitting requirements because they’re mobile. The company also argued that the plaintiffs did not have the standing to sue.

“Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s [State Implementation Plan], and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed,” Judge Debra M. Brown wrote in her decision .

Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”

TechCrunch has reached out to SpaceX for comment.

In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month )

“The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution,” Connor said. “Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”

The NAACP lawsuit is moving forward as public opinion seems to have turned sharply against data centers, with New York recently passing a moratorium on new data centers and other state and local governments considering similar measures.

The backlash also prompted Amazon and Microsoft to promise to stop using NDAs in their dealings with government agencies, and it could be a significant factor in the imminent U.S. midterm elections .

articles.title: Stanford scientists watched African killifish for their entire lives; despite similar genes and conditions, early swimming and sleep patterns predicted lifespan
articles.summary: Research from Stanford University shows that early behavioral patterns in African turquoise killifish, such as swimming and sleep habits, can predict their lifespan. The study reveals a complex relationship between activity levels and longevity, uncovering distinct behavioral stages of aging in fish.
articles.body: Two African turquoise killifish of the same age, raised under a carefully controlled environment, could take different developmental trajectories into their maturity. One may grow up to be active, swim vigorously and concentrate most of its sleep at night. Meanwhile, the other might gradually become less active and spend more time resting during daylight hours. Stanford University researchers found that these behavioural differences could emerge very early in adulthood and help predict whether an individual fish would have a shorter or longer lifespan. The scientists also discovered, while continuously monitoring the animals from adolescence until death, that ageing involved distinct periods of behavioural stability interrupted by relatively abrupt transitions.A camera system followed fish from adolescence to deathThe researchers picked the African turquoise killifish, a small vertebrate that usually lives for just four to eight months in laboratory conditions. The naturally compressed lifespan of the species makes it possible to study changes associated with ageing over a shorter time period than what would be required for longer-lived animals. Despite having a short lifespan, the fish has a complex brain and various biological characteristics that make it useful for testing vertebrate ageing.The findings were published in Science in 2026, and the experiment was led by Claire Bedbrook and Ravi Nath. The Stanford researchers developed an automated system that housed individual fish in separate tanks and documented their behaviour constantly. After reaching maturity, the animals were placed in the system at approximately three to four weeks of age. The overhead cameras set up for the experiment recorded their movements at 20 frames per second, thus allowing the team to follow each fish throughout its adult life. A cohort of 81 fish were included for the principal whole-lifespan behavioural analysis and were recorded for an average of 220 days. Their observed lifespans ranged from 23 to 371 days.In addition, computer vision and machine-learning techniques to analyse the recordings were used by the researchers. They identified 100 recurring behavioural patterns, which they called “behavioural syllables.” Therefore, by organising the documented information into daily behavioural patterns, the crew could compare how individual fish evolved and identify differences between animals that lived shorter or longer lives.Swimming and sleep patterns showed early hintsOne of the most significant findings included the behavioural trajectories of longer-lived and shorter-lived fish. The behaviour started diverging while the animals were still relatively young. The team noted that prediction models performed poorly at ages below 70 days but improved after that point. By around 70-110 days, behavioural differences were sufficiently visible for machine-learning models to distinguish between fish that would eventually fall into shorter-or longer-lifespan groups.Among other differences, sleep and rest patterns were the clearest of them. Fish that ultimately lived shorter lives increasingly spent more time in sleep-like or inactive states during daylight hours. Meanwhile, those that tended to concentrate these states at night showed a clearly defined daily rhythm. Additionally, the researchers noted differences in movement. Fish with longer lifespans usually displayed more vigorous daytime activity and reached higher levels of swimming speed when moving in the tanks.These daily behavioural measurements were used by the team to place fish into shorter- or longer-lived categories. The shorter-lived group consisted of fish that died before 200 days but lived at least 120 days. This excluded those that died prematurely. For fish that survived past the early baseline, the models achieved useful predictive performance using behavioural data collected at 70, 90 and 110 days. Instead of calculating the exact death date for each fish, the researchers estimated which lifespan category an individual was more likely to belong to.Ageing unfolded through distinct behavioural stagesThe continuous recordings also contested the idea that ageing necessarily appears as a smooth, gradual decline. When the researchers analysed each fish’s behaviour across its lifespan, they found periods when daily activity patterns remained relatively stable, followed by abrupt transitions into different behavioural states. Many of the animals experienced between two and six such transitions. These stages were identified through statistical modelling of behavioural patterns rather than being established as universal biological stages that every fish must experience in exactly same way.The team also tested gene expression across eight organs to see whether the behavioural differences were reflected in the body’s molecular activity. The liver in particular showed pronounced differences between fish following shorter- and longer-lifespan trajectories. They identified changes in groups of genes linked with cellular processes, including production of protein and maintenance. While these findings drew a connection between observable behaviour and organ-specific molecular differences, they did not demonstrate that the liver change directly caused the different lifespan.

articles.title: A spacecraft flew through a strange S-shaped twist in space; scientists traced it back to the Sun
articles.summary: The Solar Orbiter spacecraft has unveiled the origins of mysterious S-shaped twists in the Sun's magnetic field, revealing key insights that connect solar phenomena to the solar wind and the Sun's atmosphere.
articles.body: Somewhere between Earth and the Sun, a spacecraft drifted through an S-shaped bend in the solar magnetic field. The European Space Agency’s (ESA) report on the findings, published on 8th October 2026, said the clues pointed to the Sun’s lowest atmosphere. According to the ESA report on the Nature Astronomy study, Solar Orbiter was roughly halfway between Earth and the Sun when it crossed the switchback and its Solar Wind Analyser picked up a mix of charged oxygen and carbon particles that could only have formed in hot magnetic loops. Those fingerprints pointed to interchange reconnection in the Sun’s atmosphere, while the plasma’s later motion still showed the hallmarks of the waves and turbulence.Solar Orbiter’s flight through a very large switchbackThis magnetic field is mobile. It is carried away from the Sun by a constant flow of hot charged particles known as the solar wind. These field lines are not always straight; they can break, twist or even fold back. When this occurs sharply, it is referred to as a switchback. The new work comes from the study On the Coronal Origin of Magnetic Switchbacks in the Solar Wind, published in Nature Astronomy and led by Jesse Coburn of CNRS/LPP in France. According to Coburn, this is where the Solar Orbiter sampled rare particles within this massive switchback structure. The paper reports measurements from Solar Orbiter at 0.55AU, using heavy-ion data to trace the structure’s source. Elevated oxygen and carbon charge-state ratios, together with a relative helium depletion, indicate the plasma came from hot closed coronal loops and the author says a semi-empirical coronal model links it to either a coronal-hole boundary or loops within the hole.Oxygen and carbon ions that point to hot magnetic loopsThere were charged oxygen and carbon ions in the plasma. The mix of ions meant the plasma was created in hot magnetic loops in the Sun’s lower atmosphere. Coburn referred to the mix of ions as the “smoking gun” for the process of interchange reconnection. In some parts of the solar atmosphere, the field lines are open and they extend into space. However, in other regions, there are closed loops which bend back toward the Sun. When an open region is close to a closed one, the field lines may come together and break and reconnect, allowing the plasma from the loop to escape.Waves and turbulence appear to shape the journeyThe alternative theory focuses on waves and turbulence. As for the above-mentioned study, it shows that this phenomenon has been observed but probably only after the switchback has travelled out of the solar atmosphere. According to Stephanienn Yardley, co-author of the study from Northumbria University in the UK, waves and turbulence govern the structure’s dynamics once it has travelled away from the Sun.Thus, the two theories may describe different phases of a single switchback’s evolution. To determine its origin, scientists had to examine images of the Sun’s disc and develop models for its magnetic fields, both solar and interplanetary.A switchback first spotted in the corona in 2022This was not the first time a Solar Orbiter had caught one. The Observation of a Magnetic Switchback in the Solar Corona study, published in Astrophysical Journal Letters in 2022 and led by Daniele Telloni, reported images from the spacecraft’s Metis coronagraph. Researchers observed a single, large, propagating S-shaped vortex, which they interpreted as possible evidence of a magnetic switchback in the solar corona. It originated from an active region, in which a set of loops existed between the open field regions on its eastern and western edges. The researchers led by Telloni also highlighted that Parker Solar Probe had already found the switchbacks extensively in interplanetary space, but the nature of the process and origins still remain unanswered. Their observations, simulations and theories provide substantial evidence about the interchange reconnection process. The ESA also noted that the 2022 discovery confirmed the S-shaped structure that scientists had proposed earlier.What the findings mean for solar stormsThe finding offers insight into how the Sun heats its atmosphere and drives charged particles away from the star. In addition, this finding indicates that the Sun’s atmosphere is imprinted onto the particles of the solar wind, potentially allowing for reconstruction of the history of the solar plasma at a great distance from the Sun. Daniel Müller, ESA Project Scientist for Solar Orbiter, stated that the solar wind connects Earth and the Sun and that studying it will help prepare for solar storms.

articles.title: A study of 509 wild snakes across the southeastern US uncovers two infections linked to poorer nutritional condition, including a fungus and an invasive parasite
articles.summary: Wild snakes in the southeastern United States face health risks from a fungal disease and an invasive parasite that can affect their skin and respiratory
articles.body: Wild snakes in the southeastern United States face health risks from a fungal disease and an invasive parasite that can affect their skin and respiratory system. A study examined 509 snakes from 29 species and found evidence of both infections, which researchers linked to poorer nutritional condition.The fungus was detected in 16.1% of tested snakes, while the parasite was found in 12.7% of those tested in Florida. The findings also showed that some snakes carried several pathogens at once. According to research published in Frontiers in Veterinary Science titled ‘Health assessment and multipathogen surveillance of free-ranging snakes in the southeastern United States’, the results provide a baseline for understanding disease in local wild snake populations and guiding conservation work.Researchers examined snakes across five southeastern US statesThe researchers examined free-ranging snakes at wetland sites in Volusia County, Florida, and Jasper County, South Carolina, from May 2022 to May 2024. They also included snakes collected in Athens-Clarke County, Georgia, and diagnostic cases submitted between 2021 and 2024 from several states, including Louisiana and Tennessee. The team captured animals through visual searches, road surveys, cover boards, and minnow traps. Researchers physically examined each snake and, where possible, collected skin, mouth, and cloacal swabs, as well as blood and faecal samples.In total, the study included 509 snakes representing 29 species, including 61 carcasses assessed after death. The team tested samples for seven pathogen groups to build a broader picture of snake health in the region over time.How was the fungal infection associated with snakes' nutritional conditionThe fungus Ophidiomyces ophidiicola causes a disease known as ophidiomycosis, which can produce skin lesions such as misshapen scales, crusting, and ulcers. The researchers detected the fungus in 16.1% of tested snakes, or 82 of 508 samples. Skin lesions were recorded in 45.9% of examined snakes, although not every lesion was linked to this fungus.Among snakes with lesions, 30.5% tested positive for the pathogen. The study found that pygmy rattlesnakes had a higher likelihood of fungal detection and apparent ophidiomycosis than several other species. Severe cases can affect internal organs and may lead to death. The researchers found that fungal detection was associated with poorer nutritional condition in snakes. Researchers used laboratory tests alongside visible signs to assess infection.Invasive pentastome found in the lungs, windpipe, and body cavitiesThe second infection involved Raillietiella orientalis, an invasive parasite known as a pentastome. It was detected in 12.7% of the Florida snakes tested, or 37 of 292 samples. The parasite was not detected in snakes sampled at the South Carolina or Georgia sites. Adult parasites can occur in the oral cavity, windpipe, and lungs, as well as within the body cavity.The researchers noted that the parasite was likely introduced to South Florida by invasive Burmese pythons and has since spread among native snakes. In six snakes examined after death at the Florida site, all had pentastomiasis, with between 4 and 12 adult parasites found in different body locations.What did researchers find about multiple infections in wild snakesOverall, 44% of tested snakes had more than one pathogen. Snakes with several infections were more likely to show signs of fungal disease. Detection of the fungus, and separately of the parasite, was associated with lower nutritional condition scores. Pygmy rattlesnakes showed high detection rates for the fungus and parasite among the species examined.The findings do not represent every snake habitat in the southeastern United States. Most live sampling took place at two wetland sites, and capture methods may favour some species over others. According to the researchers, further research is needed to understand how infections affect populations over time and to support monitoring and conservation efforts across the region.

articles.title: NASA's new satellite images show an Antarctic island that looks like a giant skull, with a rocky eye socket and glacier jaw; the October 2026 view reveals more bare ice after an unusually warm winter
articles.summary: From high above the Weddell Sea, Vega Island appears to be staring back at Earth.
articles.body: From high above the Weddell Sea, Vega Island appears to be staring back at Earth. NASA’s latest satellite images show a section of the ice-covered Antarctic island shaped like a grinning skull in profile, complete with a rocky eye socket, a dark glacial mouth and a jawbone formed by ice. But beneath the striking visual is a more serious message: the October 2026 image reveals unusually large areas of bare ice after a warmer-than-average Antarctic winter, according to NASA Earth Observatory.A skull made by natureVega Island lies east of the Antarctic Peninsula, a remote and ice-bound outpost in the Weddell Sea. From the right angle, its natural features combine into an unsettling likeness of a human skull looking toward nearby Devil Island. A nunatak, a rocky peak protruding through the ice, forms the eye socket, while a lateral moraine creates the appearance of a mouth. Bahía del Diablo, or Devil’s Bay Glacier, supplies the jawbone.NASA Earth Observatory published the comparison on 30 October 2026, using images captured by the Operational Land Imager on Landsat 9. The earlier image, taken on 22 March 2025, shows the island near the start of the austral autumn, when a layer of seasonal snow covered much of the ice. The newer image, acquired on 10 October 2026, shows a very different surface, with large grey areas where snow has disappeared and darker bare ice is exposed.The effect is powerful because the skull is not a single landform but a collection of ice, rock and debris arranged by nature. In the 2025 view, snow softens the features and makes the island look more uniformly white. In the 2026 view, the exposed ice sharpens the “face,” making the eye socket and jaw appear more pronounced.Why more ice is visibleGlaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College told NASA that above-average temperatures during the 2026 winter, particularly in June, helped explain the unusually extensive bare ice. Limited new snow accumulation over the winter, combined with sublimation and wind scouring, left more of the glacier surface exposed by October. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers,” Pelto said.That matters because bare ice behaves very differently from snow. Snow is bright and reflects much of the Sun’s energy back into the atmosphere, while bare ice is darker and absorbs more solar radiation. As Antarctic days lengthen and temperatures rise into the melt season, that darker surface can accelerate melting, creating a feedback loop in which exposed ice warms faster and loses mass more quickly.Pelto noted that even a thin spring snowfall would help in the short term by insulating the glacier surface. But if the ice remains exposed, the skull-like features may gradually change. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved,” he told NASA. “But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”A longer record of retreatThe skull may look new in satellite imagery, but scientists have been studying Vega Island’s glaciers for decades. The first comprehensive mapping of its ice was supported by early Landsat observations, aerial photographs and topographic maps. A study published in 1982 catalogued 29 glaciers on the island and described its four ice caps, rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers.One of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier, has been monitored closely since the austral summer of 1998 to 1999. Researchers have measured an overall decline in its mass over that period. Satellite images from recent decades also show ice loss from other glaciers on Vega Island, alongside an increase in exposed bedrock.In other words, the October 2026 image is not simply a seasonal snapshot. It fits into a longer pattern of change on the Antarctic Peninsula, where warming conditions, reduced snow accumulation and longer exposure of glacier ice can combine to alter the landscape over time.An island with a dramatic pastVega Island’s eerie appearance has an echo in its exploration history. During the Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901 to 1903, teams studying the geography, geology, climate and wildlife around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula became separated into three groups. They spent a winter isolated in different locations after their ship was lost to pack ice.Cape Well-met, off what looks like the forehead of the island’s skull, became the site of a reunion between two of those groups in the spring of 1903. Soon afterwards, an Argentine expedition rescued the survivors. The name of the cape reflects that moment of relief after a prolonged and dangerous ordeal.What the image tells usThe skull-like island is a reminder that satellite imagery can reveal both beauty and warning. The visual is created by ordinary glacial processes, but the growing extent of bare ice points to conditions that could make the coming melt season more intense. NASA’s images show that Vega Island’s “face” is not fixed; it changes as snow arrives, melts, blows away or fails to accumulate.For scientists, the value lies in the detail. Landsat allows researchers to compare the same landscape across seasons and years, tracking snow cover, glacier extent and exposed rock. For everyone else, the image offers a vivid way to understand a distant corner of Antarctica: an island that looks like a skull, and whose changing surface may reveal how its glaciers are responding to a warming climate.NASA's new satellite images show an Antarctic island that looks like a giant skull, with a rocky eye socket and glacier jaw; the October 2026 view reveals more bare ice after an unusually warm winter

articles.title: Astronomers look inside a 1,600-year-old supernova remnant and find 2 hot cores linked to newborn stars
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered two newborn stars growing within the wreckage of a 1,600-year-old exploded star, offering insights into star formation and the survival of organic molecules in harsh cosmic environments.
articles.body: When a massive star explodes, it tends to leave chaos behind. Shocks sweep past, cosmic rays are accelerated and nearby gas and dust are reshaped. It is surprising, then, to find wreckage of such a blast hosting newborn stars. The ALMA Observatory’s press release, dated 13 July 2026, described exactly that inside RX J1713.7-3946, a remnant left by a massive star that, according to the release, exploded about 1,600 years ago.Two hot cores inside the remnant RX J1713.7-3946 This remnant is called RX J1713.7-3946. Takashi Shimonishi from Niigata University, along with his team, directed the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) towards this remnant to look out for hot cores, which are warm and dense shells of molecular gases that surround baby stars. Astronomers studying records from China’s Jin dynasty have long linked the remnant to a “guest star” seen in 393 AD, though a 2012 study in The Astronomical Journal questioned how well the two match.The results appear in the study Survival of Molecular Complexity under Recent Supernova Feedback: Detection of Hot Cores in RX J1713.7-3946, by Takashi Shimonishi, Hidetoshi Sano, Kenji Furuya and Yoko Oya, published in The Astrophysical Journal. ALMA detected two hot cores, which the ALMA press release describes as the first detection of hot molecular cores in a supernova remnant. Both show rich molecular emission, including a wide variety of organic molecules. The paper reports that ALMA identified two hot cores, HC1 and HC2, inside the remnant’s X-ray shell, both tied to Class I intermediate-mass protostars. Focusing on HC1, the authors detected a suite of carbon-, oxygen-, nitrogen-, sulphur- and silicon-bearing species and their excitation analysis put the gas at roughly 10⁷ cm⁻³, under 500 au across, and above 100 K. The authors argue the shocks may have reached the material too recently to erase that chemistry or that amplified magnetic fields may be shielding it from enhanced cosmic rays.Chemistry that survived the blastOrganic molecules may form due to chemical reactions on the surface of dust grains in molecular clouds where conditions are extremely cold. Once a young star forms and heats its surroundings, that ice evaporates into gas, which is how hot cores are detected.Analysis of HC1 shows that its complex organic molecules are present in proportions similar to those in hot cores in star-forming regions untouched by nearby supernovae. Such an outcome was not guaranteed, since the destruction or synthesis of organic molecules could have occurred in response to energetic particles and shock waves.Why the molecules may have lastedTwo explanations are suggested by the scientists. First is the timing issue. The supernova shock may have reached the cores only recently, leaving too little time for energetic particles to significantly alter their chemistry. The second explanation has something to do with the magnetic field. The shock wave from the supernova supposedly increases the magnetic field in the cloud, which in turn prevents the rays from penetrating into the denser parts. Shimonishi suggests that the observations indicate how newly formed stars may remain protected within their surrounding environments, despite the harsh conditions. But whether this is usually happening is still unknown.A star-forming region flagged back in 2010Star formation in this region was suspected long before ALMA looked. The 2010 study Star-forming Dense Cloud Cores in the TeV Gamma-ray SNR RX J1713.7-3946, led by Hiroaki Sano and also published in The Astrophysical Journal, examined molecular cloud cores in the remnant. The paper’s abstract says a core labelled peak C shows clear evidence of active star formation, including bipolar outflow. They say the core survived the shockwave and remains within the remnant and that simulations suggest a dense clump can withstand shock erosion. In the Shimonishi paper, the two fields of study for ALMA are explained as being peak C and D of the aforementioned research paper.What it could mean for the Solar SystemThe finding also has broader implications. Niigata University’s announcement says that the Solar System could have originated from a place that was heavily affected by neighbouring supernovae. In addition to this, the press release from ALMA states that the chemically rich core of RX J1713.7-3946 can provide a valuable analogy in researching how the influence of supernovae on star and planet-forming ingredients works. Shimonishi also stated that places that are capable of having complex organic molecules, which are potentially important for prebiotic chemistry, may be more diverse than has been known before.

articles.title: A new fossil from China may reveal the first amphibian known to have lived entirely at sea; the armoured, 2.4-foot creature lived about 237 million years ago, challenging what scientists know about amphibian evolution
articles.summary: Whenever we think of amphibians, we usually picture animals that live both on land and in water, such as frogs, salamanders and newts.
articles.body: Whenever we think of amphibians, we usually picture animals that live both on land and in water, such as frogs, salamanders and newts. Their ability to survive in both environments is one of the defining features of the group. But what if an amphibian once lived entirely in the sea? A newly described fossil from China may offer evidence of just that. Dating back around 237 million years, the armoured creature measured approximately 2.4 feet in length and could challenge what scientists have long understood about amphibian evolution.The newly identified species, named Gerrothorax maritimus, lived during the Late Triassic period. Researchers examined two nearly complete fossilised skeletons discovered in what is now China's Guizhou Province, an area that was once covered by the sea. The findings, published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, provide the first fossil evidence of a stem amphibian that may have lived entirely in a marine environment.What did the ancient marine amphibian look like?Unlike the amphibians we are familiar with today, Gerrothorax maritimus had a flattened, disc-shaped body covered in layers of bony armour. Measuring around 74 centimetres, or approximately 2.4 feet, it was roughly the size of a large salamander. Its broad body and protective covering made it quite different from modern amphibians, which generally have soft, permeable skin.Researchers believe the animal was a bottom-dwelling creature that lived close to the seabed. Its broad head and mouth, along with its small conical teeth, suggest that it may have fed by sucking in smaller animals that passed nearby. The armour may also have offered protection against predators, including large marine reptiles such as ichthyosaurs, whose fossils have been found in the same region.Why is finding an amphibian living entirely at sea so unusual?One of the biggest reasons this discovery is interesting is that amphibians are generally not suited to living in saltwater. Unlike reptiles, birds and mammals, most amphibians have highly permeable skin that allows them to absorb water and exchange gases with their surroundings. While this works well in freshwater environments, exposure to seawater can cause them to lose water through their skin, leading to dehydration.Even among the more than 8,000 living amphibian species, none is known to live entirely in a marine environment. Some, such as the crab-eating frog, can tolerate a certain amount of saltwater exposure, but they still need access to freshwater to recover. This has long made a fully marine amphibian seem unlikely.However, researchers believe Gerrothorax maritimus may have overcome this limitation through its unusual body structure. Its extensive bony armour could have restricted the movement of water and salts through its skin, reducing its dependence on the usual amphibian method of absorbing water. Instead, it may have relied more heavily on its mouth and digestive system to take in water, while its gills helped regulate salt levelsHow did scientists establish that it lived in the sea?The researchers did not rely on the location of the fossils alone. Both skeletons were found in deep-sea sediments, hundreds of miles from major landmasses that existed during the Late Triassic period. Their relatively complete condition was also important. The researchers suggest that the animals probably died close to where they lived, rather than being carried into the sea after death, as their skeletons still preserved delicate parts such as the fingers.The team also conducted geochemical tests on the fossils, examining the proportions of different strontium isotopes preserved in the bones. Strontium isotope ratios can provide clues about the environment in which an animal lived. In this case, the results closely matched the composition of seawater from the Late Triassic period, supporting the idea that these amphibians grew up in the ocean rather than simply ending up there by accident.The researchers believe Gerrothorax maritimus descended from a lineage of amphibians that already possessed extensive body armour but lived in freshwater environments. Its close relative, Gerrothorax pulcherrimus, also had a flattened body and bony covering, but was not known to have lived in the sea.This raises an interesting possibility: features that originally evolved for protection may have eventually helped some members of the group adapt to an entirely different environment. The armour may have reduced the problems associated with saltwater exposure, allowing the animal to survive in conditions that would be difficult for most amphibians today.The discovery actually reminds us there are so many mysteries yet to be unwound. It shows that their evolutionary history may have been more varied than scientists previously understood. It also offers another example of how evolution can repurpose existing features, sometimes allowing animals to occupy environments that once seemed impossible for their ancestors.

articles.body: A river in Tennessee, US, that was straightened more than a century ago to drain surrounding land is now being prepared for restoration after years of flooding problems. Authorities have acquired 985 acres along the South Fork of the Forked Deer River near Jackson, where changes made to the river in 1916 have contributed to flash floods, erosion and sand deposits in nearby areas. The project, announced on Thursday, aims to reconnect the river with its natural floodplain, reduce future flooding and eventually open the restored land to the public.The work will be carried out by the West Tennessee River Basin Authority, which is preparing a plan to restore the river and the land around it. According to the National Wildlife Federation, the project will focus on allowing water to spread across the floodplain rather than remaining confined to the river's modified channel. Officials believe this will help protect communities in East Jackson and Bemis, where flooding has remained a concern.The problem began in 1916, when engineers decided to straighten the South Fork of the Forked Deer River to drain low-lying land around Jackson. The river was channelised, a process in which its natural course is modified to direct water through a more controlled channel. The changes were intended to improve drainage, but they also altered how the river interacted with the surrounding land.Over time, the modified river contributed to repeated flash floods, damaged infrastructure and deposits of sand in low-lying areas. Efforts to manage these problems have continued for decades, but the difficulties have remained. Authorities now plan to address them by restoring the river's connection with its historic floodplain, allowing water to move through the surrounding landscape more naturally.Changing the river againThe land beside a river that can become submerged during flooding is known as a floodplain. Such areas allow excess water to spread beyond the main river channel. Reconnecting the South Fork of the Forked Deer River with its floodplain is expected to slow the movement of water and reduce the damage caused by sudden flooding.The West Tennessee River Basin Authority also expects the work to reduce erosion and sediment pollution. These problems occur when flowing water carries soil and other material from one area and deposits it elsewhere.David Blackwood, executive director of the authority, said the project would help address several problems affecting the Jackson area.“Rivers need room, and channelised rivers are limited. By reconnecting the river to the floodplain, we can reduce challenges like flash flooding and sediment pollution, improving water quality, wildlife habitat and our quality of life in the Jackson area.”However, officials have cautioned that the restoration will not completely prevent flooding. Speaking to WBBJ-TV, Blackwood said the project would improve how the floodplain functions and lower flood risks, but would not eliminate them.What makes the 985-acre property important?The land selected for restoration lies on the southern side of Jackson, below US Highway 70 and west of US Highway 45.It was previously owned by the Jones Family Trust. Two conservation organisations, The Nature Conservancy and The Conservation Fund, purchased the property in 2025 before transferring it to the State of Tennessee through a sale in 2026.Apart from its importance in managing floodwater, the property contains natural habitats that have become less widespread in West Tennessee. These include cypress swamps, cane brakes and bottomland hardwood forests.The restoration will seek to improve conditions for these habitats while allowing the river and its surrounding waterways to function more naturally.Laurel Creech, Tennessee state director for The Nature Conservancy, said the work would help bring back natural processes that had been disrupted for generations.According to the National Wildlife Federation, similar river restoration efforts elsewhere in the region have been followed by increases in wildlife diversity, including fish, amphibians, birds and mammals.What happens next?Although the land has been acquired, the restoration work is still being planned. The West Tennessee River Basin Authority is developing a timeline and deciding how the river, tributaries and surrounding waterways should be redesigned.The immediate priority is reducing flood risks, particularly for East Jackson and Bemis. Plans for public access will follow once the work needed to improve water movement has been addressed.Residents will then be invited to participate in discussions about how the restored property should be used. Officials want the area to provide opportunities for outdoor recreation and education about rivers and floodplains.According to WBBJ-TV, representatives from Jackson, Madison County, the Tennessee state government and the river basin authority met at the Greater Jackson Chamber on Thursday to discuss progress. The project also includes efforts to improve water quality and protect the Memphis sands aquifer.
