articles.title: Can odors from our bodies signal Alzheimer's, cancer and other diseases?
articles.summary: When social anthropologist Hanna Marie Ihlebæk interviewed nurses at a Norwegian cancer ward for her PhD dissertation, she was surprised to learn that many o...
articles.body:
When social anthropologist Hanna Marie Ihlebæk interviewed nurses at a Norwegian cancer ward for her PhD dissertation, she was surprised to learn that many of them relied on their sense of smell in their work. "Urine infection is really distinct, I can recognize that smell in the corridor!" one of the nurses said. Another claimed to be able to pick out digestive bleeding and cell necrosis. "I don't know what I would have done without my ability to smell," said a third.

Long ago, in the 5th century B.C., the Greek physician-philosopher Hippocrates held that disease could be identified by body odor. In modern times, we have stories of Oscar the cat who seemed to perceive which residents would soon die at a Rhode Island nursing home, and dogs that have been used to detect bladder cancer, malaria and covid. In Africa, giant pouched rats are employed to sniff out tuberculosis.

For years, scientists have explored how the molecules that waft from our breath or skin might be harnessed to sniff out a laundry list of diseases - Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, certain cancers, the flu and the common cold. Yet the field has struggled to bring such tests to the clinic. Now, with new tools that can detect tiny amounts of molecules, as well as advances in machine learning, that goal appears within reach. A variety of ailments might soon be efficiently diagnosed with noninvasive tests that employ devices as simple as Breathalyzers.

"It's really, really exciting," says Mark Woollam, a chemical biologist at the University of Indianapolis.

A handful of breath-based tests are already in use, such as one that detects gastric infection by Helicobacter pylori , a major cause of stomach ulcers. Patients drink a solution spiked with urea containing a "heavy" version of carbon; if H. pylori is present, the bacterium will use the urea to make carbon dioxide and the test will detect that heavy-carbon CO2 in the patients' breath. But tests like that require swallowing a special substance and shipping a sample to a lab for analysis. Today, researchers are also working to develop tests that could give results directly at home, or at a doctor's office. They are designed to sniff out volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Such compounds are mostly in gas form at room temperature and can be emitted from breath, sweat, urine, blood and fecal matter.

To collect breath for analysis, for example, volunteers breathe into small, lab-grade plastic bags that resemble juice pouches, or into syringe-like breath samplers. Such samples are then analyzed in a lab with a technique called gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Other tests employ cheaper and more portable electronic noses, which are made of a series of sensors that can pick out various molecules.

Figuring out what molecules are significant and what conclusions can be drawn from an individual sample makes the development of such tests "very, very challenging," Woollam says. Breath can contain contaminants from the surrounding air (think pollution or cigarette smoke), and the composition of breath can vary from one moment to another, making it hard to standardize tests and interpret single measurements.

"From sitting to lying, you change your breath profile. You hold your breath, you change your breath profile. You take a drug, you change your breath profile. … So how do you want to sort that out?" says chemist Wolfram Miekisch, of the University Medical Center Rostock in Germany.

But researchers have made progress in pinpointing molecules that are markers of specific diseases. When tumors grow, for example, oxidative stress in the body increases, which leads to the breakdown of fatty molecules within cells into smaller, volatile compounds, Woollam says.

In one study, testing the breath of patients before and after a surgery to remove lung tumors identified 16 such compounds that might serve as lung cancer breath biomarkers, including pentanal, foul-smelling butyric acid, woody hexanal and decanal, which smells like orange peel. In other research, analyses of molecules emitted from melanoma biopsy samples suggested that compounds such as the pungent chemical called 4-methyl decane could serve as a biomarker.

Molecules in urine could also offer clues to cancer. Woollam and colleagues analyzed molecules wafting from the urine of men undergoing a prostate cancer biopsy and found that a panel of six molecules could detect the disease in 75 percent of cases. While it's less sensitive than the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood-based test, the VOC method gave fewer false positives, which could help patients avoid unnecessary treatment.

Some cancer tests based on volatile compounds emanating from urine may soon hit the market. One such test by the biotech company TOBY - named after the trail-sniffing dog in Sherlock Holmes books - is designed to detect bladder cancer. Rather than looking for a single biomarker, TOBY's test uses AI to analyze patterns of molecules wafting from urine. It was granted Breakthrough Device designation (which can speed up approval) by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2026, validating its potential; its developers say it is about a year away from commercial launch. The TOBY team is also working on a similar test for Alzheimer's, which received the FDA's Breakthrough Device designation in May.

Clues to disease also reside in sebum, an oily, sticky substance produced by tiny glands in hair follicles. Researchers are investigating the link between volatiles emanating from sebum and Parkinson's disease, which tends to be diagnosed late, meaning patients go longer without their symptoms being properly managed.

Hints of the sebum signal emerged many years ago: A woman named Joy Milne noticed that her husband's body odor had turned unpleasantly woody and musky. Fourteen years later, Les Milne was diagnosed with early-onset Parkinson's disease, and at a Parkinson's awareness lecture, Joy Milne noticed that the other Parkinson's patients seemed to have a similar odor. She connected with scientists at the University of Edinburgh, and then with Parkinson's researcher Perdita Barran. Barran and her team ran an experiment and found that Milne's nose could distinguish T-shirts worn by Parkinson's patients from those worn by healthy people.

Since then, Milne and Barran, at the University of Manchester, have worked together to identify a Parkinson's signal in the sebum molecules. "If I swabbed your back, I would find about 20,000 compounds. And if you had Parkinson's, about 2,000 of them - so, 10 percent - would be different to people who don't have Parkinson's," Barran says. These compounds include acyl-carnitines - molecules that shuttle fatty acids into mitochondria for energy production - and others linked to perturbations in fatty acid metabolism.

The sebum signature can correctly identify over 84 percent of people with Parkinson's when the disease is well underway. But the test also may help spot Parkinson's early on, before clear-cut symptoms appear. In a 2025 report, Barran and her colleagues, including Milne, studied the sebum of people who have REM sleep behavior disorder, in which they physically act out their dreams - kicking their spouse in bed while dreaming of playing soccer, for example. This condition has been strongly linked to the later development of neurodegenerative conditions. Sebum VOC profiles in this group were somewhere in between those with diagnosed Parkinson's disease and healthy volunteers, the researchers reported.

And other tests may be on the horizon. Researchers are probing potential breath signatures for the flu for example; one 2022 study, examining 235 patients, found that some breath biomarkers could distinguish the flu from similar infections with 78 percent accuracy. Exhaled breath might also be used to diagnose infections with the common cold: Another team found that concentrations of compounds such as waxy-smelling 3,8-dimethylundecane in breath correlate with rhinovirus viral loads in the nose and throat.

"What the virus does, it goes to a cell, enters the cell, replicates itself, and then blasts the cell," Miekisch says. Parts of the destroyed cell may then be emitted in a sick person's breath, he explains, while other biomarkers come from the changes within our own metabolism in response to the infection.

Still other researchers are looking for ways to discern viral infections from bacterial ones. Bacteria emit their own VOCs, which can be picked up in human breath ( Helicobacter pylori , the bacterium behind stomach ulcers, smells sulfurous, for example). Ilaria Belluomo, a medical biotechnologist at Imperial College London, and her colleagues are running a study on bacterial and viral signatures in the breath of children hospitalized for severe lung infections. "A test that can discriminate the two types of infections can be completely transformative," she says. By revealing whether an infection is bacterial, it would help discern whether taking antibiotics makes sense, potentially reducing antibiotic overuse, Belluomo says.

One of the most promising applications of research on volatile biomarkers of infection would be in the ICU, Miekisch says. It could make it possible to continuously monitor the breath of intubated, critically ill patients to spot early signs of danger. For example, distinguishing between sepsis, which is caused by bacteria, and the autoimmune reaction called systemic inflammatory response syndrome is "an important question," he says.

Yet obstacles remain. One is a lack of standardization, so it is difficult to compare results between different studies. Another hurdle is not having a good grasp on where these biomarkers are coming from, Miekisch says. And some tests that looked promising went on to fail in larger studies or lacked the funding to get to market.

But many VOC scientists remain optimistic. "Although VOC research has faced numerous challenges, the field continues to make remarkable progress," Woollam says. Perhaps patients won't have to hold their breath for too long, after all.

Marta Zaraska is a Canadian-Polish-French science journalist based in France. This article was produced in collaboration with Knowable Magazine .

articles.title: Former Pentagon UFO chief disputes FBI black triangle sighting, says reports lack evidence
articles.summary: The former Pentagon UFO office chief says the FBI's triangular object sighting lacks evidence, calling witness credibility a "classic authority bias."
articles.body: The former head of the Pentagon's UFO investigation office is pouring cold water on a mysterious black triangular object reportedly spotted by FBI personnel, telling Fox News Digital that the newly released account lacks the evidence needed to determine what the witnesses actually saw. Sean Kirkpatrick, the former director of the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO), said strange sightings detailed in recently declassified government records should be viewed through an evidence-based lens rather than as proof of something extraterrestrial. The records include a 2026 sighting involving FBI personnel who reported seeing a dark, nonreflective triangular object with no visible engines, exhaust or conventional propulsion system rise above a mountain ridge before rapidly disappearing into a canyon. NEW TRUMP UFO FILE DUMP INCLUDES MILITARY FOOTAGE OF MYSTERIOUS STAR-SHAPED OBJECT A separate AARO report described a matte-black triangular object that climbed about 200 to 300 feet above the ridgeline, hovered for roughly 20 seconds and then appeared to accelerate almost instantly. Kirkpatrick, who spent nearly 30 years in the Department of Defense and intelligence community, said the witnesses' FBI backgrounds alone are not enough to validate what they reported seeing. NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS "There's a lot of people that like to point to folks as being credible witnesses and therefore their testimony must be taken at face value," Kirkpatrick told Fox News Digital. "And that is a classic case of authority bias." Kirkpatrick said the lack of photographs or other supporting evidence makes it difficult to determine what, if anything, the witnesses encountered. NEIL DEGRASSE TYSON DARES GOVERNMENT TO 'JUST SHOW THE ALIEN,' AS DISCLOSURE FERVOR CONTINUES TO GROW "Some of this is just, ‘hey, I saw something, I don't know what it is,’" Kirkpatrick said. "People sometimes have a tendency to fill that gap with very extreme beliefs that have time and again proven to be inaccurate and fallible." He pointed to advanced aerospace technology as one possible explanation for some triangular sightings, comparing them to reports involving the F-117 stealth aircraft before the technology became widely known. PENTAGON FILES REVEAL AGENTS' REPORTS OF 'ORBS LAUNCHING ORBS' NEAR SENSITIVE US SECURITY SITE AARO approached UAP reports by examining three broad possibilities, Kirkpatrick said: advanced technology used by a foreign adversary, ordinary objects or sensor effects that are misunderstood, or an extraterrestrial explanation. "You've got 3 very distinct buckets," Kirkpatrick said. PENTAGON’S NEW UFO FILE RELEASE LOGS NEAR-MISS AS ‘SUPER-HEATED’ ORBS APPROACH US HELICOPTER Each possibility has specific signatures that investigators can compare against data collected from a sighting, he explained. "When you get data from an observation, actual data, not just a story, you compare that data to those signatures," Kirkpatrick said. UFO INVESTIGATOR WARNS TRUMP DISCLOSURE COULD HAND SENSITIVE MILITARY SECRETS TO CHINA, RUSSIA "None of the data that we saw and reviewed and analyzed matches an alien hypothesis theory," he added. Most of the cases his office examined involved ordinary objects or phenomena that sensors were not designed to recognize. A small number showed signs of possible foreign adversary involvement and were referred to national security officials for further investigation. SECOND BATCH OF UFO FILES SET TO BE RELEASED AFTER LAWMAKER TEASED ‘HOLY CRAP’ MOMENT But the word "unresolved," which appears in government UAP records, does not necessarily mean investigators encountered something inexplicable, Kirkpatrick cautioned. "When we say a case is unresolved, it generally means there is no data or there is insufficient data to actually analyze it," Kirkpatrick said. "And so you can't conclude one way or the other." LONG-HIDDEN UFO INFORMATION AT CENTER OF TRUMP PUSH TO FREE FORMER OFFICIALS Investigators may have an idea of what an object likely was based on similar cases, he said, but without sufficient raw data, they cannot reach a definitive conclusion. Kirkpatrick said some cases released publicly as unresolved had previously been resolved by AARO. "Many of these cases, we did resolve, and I even briefed several of them to Congress with the answers and what they were and what they were likely to be," Kirkpatrick said. He said Pentagon leadership directed AARO to remove language explaining what investigators had determined before some cases were released publicly as unresolved. "Pentagon leadership had told AARO to remove all of the resolution language and put these cases out as unresolved," Kirkpatrick said. "Letting, and I quote, ‘the people make up their own mind,’ which is the absolute worst thing that you could do because all you've done is continue to just feed the flames of conspiracy with a whole bunch of nonsense." Kirkpatrick did not specify when the directive was issued or which Pentagon leaders were involved. The War Department separately told Fox News Digital that it is not providing assessments of the newly released files, allowing the public to reach its own conclusions. "We are not providing any comment or assessment on the files overall or on any specific file, so that the American people can make up their own minds regarding the files," a War Department official said on background. The department also confirmed that images accompanying the FBI triangular-object report were illustrations rather than photographs of the object itself. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Kirkpatrick said "unidentified" carries a different meaning than "unresolved," though the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. Read the report here: "Unidentified generally means we can see and characterize an object and we have data to support that characterization, but we don't know what it is," he said. He pointed to objects shot down over North America following the discovery of a Chinese surveillance balloon in 2023 as examples of objects that were initially unidentified before investigators determined they were balloons. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Other records released by the government stretch back decades, including reports of strange objects near California's Santa Catalina Island in the 1950s. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Kirkpatrick said historical sightings must also be considered alongside the technology that existed at the time, pointing to early high-altitude balloon programs as a possible explanation for some reports of bright objects in the sky. Read the Catalina Island report here: SEND US A TIP "There are thousands of these reports," Kirkpatrick said. "And so even if there were alien visitations to Earth, there are not thousands of them." GOT A TIP? The possibility of intelligent life elsewhere in the universe should not be confused with evidence that extraterrestrial beings have visited Earth, Kirkpatrick said. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST "It's statistically invalid to believe that's not going to be the case, but the probability of them being here is just as statistically unrealistic," he said. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Looking broadly at the latest records, Kirkpatrick said he saw little that changed his assessment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I mean, there's nothing new," Kirkpatrick said. Fox News Digital reached out to the FBI for comment.

articles.title: A Chester Zoo collection of Dracula orchids has been declared nationally important, drawing attention to rare flowers with bizarre, vampire-like appearances that are increasingly threatened in the wild.
articles.summary: When we hear about Dracula, the first thing that probably comes to mind is the famous vampire, with long, sharp teeth, a blood-filled mouth and a desire
articles.body: When we hear about Dracula, the first thing that probably comes to mind is the famous vampire, with long, sharp teeth, a blood-filled mouth and a desire to kill. A soft flower would probably be the last thing to come to mind, but nature has its own version of Dracula, and these are not creatures hiding deep inside dark forests, but rather some strange-looking flowers found in the cloud forests of South America.With faces that resemble monkeys, dragons and, if your mind is a little more creative, goblins from horror movies, Dracula orchids have recently attracted attention after a collection at Chester Zoo in England was recognised as a National Plant Collection, highlighting the importance of protecting these unusual flowers as their natural habitats face growing threats.The recognition was awarded by Plant Heritage, a UK-based plant conservation charity, to Chester Zoo's collection of Dracula orchids. The zoo looks after more than 75 of the 147 scientifically recognised species of these orchids, making it home to one of the most significant collections of the genus. The recognition also marks the sixth National Plant Collection held by the zoo.What makes Dracula orchids look so unusual?Despite their rather frightening name, Dracula orchids are completely harmless to humans. They belong to a genus of orchids native to the cloud forests of the Andes in Latin America, where they grow in cool, humid conditions, often among moss-covered trees and vegetation.Their flowers are what make them really fascinating. Unlike the familiar orchids that people often associate with colourful petals and elegant shapes, many Dracula orchids are known for their uncanny resemblance to a human face. Some look like monkeys, while others have the shape of a dragon. Even their name has an interesting origin. The word Dracula comes from a Latin root meaning ‘little dragon’, referring to the distinctive appearance of their flowers.One particularly unusual species that people specifically come to see at Chester Zoo is Dracula roezlii, which produces a flower that resembles a skull, giving it a spooky appearance.How do these unusual flowers attract pollinators?Their appearance is not the only interesting thing about them. Their pollination technique is equally fascinating. Unlike other flowers with sweet floral scents, these flowers give off a mushroom-like smell that attracts fungus gnats.These tiny insects are drawn towards the scent and visit the flowers, carrying pollen from one plant to another in the process. This is an example of how plants have developed different ways of attracting pollinators, sometimes using smells and appearances that humans might find rather unusual.Their very specific dependence on environmental and pollination conditions is also what makes them difficult to cultivate. According to Brie Langley, Assistant Team Manager at Chester Zoo's plant nursery, these flowers need conditions that closely resemble the cloud cover and humidity of their natural habitats. They can quickly wilt if the environment is not suitable, which also makes them difficult to display for visitors.Why are Dracula orchids increasingly threatened in the wild?Dracula orchids are native to the cloud forests of the Andes, ecosystems that are particularly sensitive to environmental changes. These forests provide the cool temperatures and consistently humid conditions that the orchids need to survive. However, habitat loss, illegal extraction and mining activities are putting pressure on these fragile environments.The problem is not limited to the destruction of their natural habitats; they are also victims of human greed. Dracula orchids are vulnerable to illegal collection, as unusual and highly sought-after species can attract collectors and traders. Removing plants from their natural habitats can further threaten already vulnerable populations, particularly when species have specific growing requirements and limited natural distributions.Chester Zoo says every Dracula orchid species in its collection faces threats from illegal extraction, habitat loss or illicit mining. The zoo's horticulturists are therefore working to safeguard these plants through cultivation and conservation efforts, helping preserve species that are increasingly difficult to protect in their natural environments.Why is Chester Zoo's collection being recognised?The National Plant Collection status is awarded by Plant Heritage to collections that are properly documented and maintained, helping preserve the diversity of cultivated plants for future generations. These collections act as living records of plant varieties and species, while also supporting research, education and conservation.Chester Zoo's Dracula orchids have received this recognition because of the number of species it maintains and their importance for conservation. The collection is particularly valuable because it brings together more than half of all scientifically recognised Dracula orchid species in one place, allowing horticulturists to study and safeguard plants that are rarely available in cultivation.However, visitors hoping to see these unusual flowers should know that the Dracula orchids are not currently on public display at the zoo. Some of its other National Plant Collections, including tropical pitcher plants and rare cactus species, can be seen by visitors.The recognition is a reminder that conservation is not limited to protecting large animals or familiar endangered species. Sometimes, it also means safeguarding small and unusual plants that most people may never have encountered, but which play their own role in the biodiversity of our natural world.

articles.title: Florida is planning 4,800 acres of wetlands at the mouth of the Kissimmee River to remove phosphorus before it reaches Lake Okeechobee, decades after engineers began undoing the river's earlier straightening
articles.summary: Nature works in mysterious ways. We knew wetlands as places that support wildlife, provide shelter to birds and fish, and help maintain ecosystems.
articles.body: Nature works in mysterious ways. We knew wetlands as places that support wildlife, provide shelter to birds and fish, and help maintain ecosystems. But did you know wetlands can also act as natural water filters? This function often goes unnoticed, but wetlands can filter water before it reaches larger water bodies by trapping excess chemicals and pollutants.Florida is doing exactly that. Florida is planning to use this natural process on a much larger scale, with a proposed 4,800-acre wetland project near the mouth of the Kissimmee River to reduce the phosphorus pollution flowing into Lake Okeechobee.The project, known as the Lower Kissimmee Basin Stormwater Treatment and Recreation Area, is being developed by the South Florida Water Management District. Located approximately three miles upstream from Lake Okeechobee, the proposed wetland system will capture and treat water from parts of the watershed that consistently record some of the highest phosphorus concentrations and pollution loads. The idea is to direct polluted stormwater through treatment areas containing aquatic vegetation, allowing plants and wetland soils to absorb and retain excess nutrients before the water reaches the lake.Why is phosphorus pollution a concern for Lake Okeechobee?Phosphorus is an important nutrient for plant growth, but excessive amounts entering freshwater ecosystems can create serious environmental problems. When too much phosphorus enters a lake, it can encourage the rapid growth of algae, including harmful blue-green algae that can affect water quality as well as aquatic life.Lake Okeechobee, one of Florida's largest freshwater lakes, has had a persistent problem with nutrient pollution over the years. Most of these nutrients run into the lake through stormwater runoff from surrounding agricultural and developed areas, carrying phosphorus and other nutrients into the lake.This excessive runoff can lead to a phenomenon known as an algal bloom. It occurs when large amounts of nutrients, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus from agricultural fertilisers and other sources, enter water bodies, encouraging the rapid growth and accumulation of algae. In freshwater ecosystems, these blooms are often caused by cyanobacteria, commonly known as blue-green algae, which can turn the water a dense green colour.Excessive algal growth can block sunlight from reaching underwater plants, affecting their ability to survive. When large amounts of algae eventually die, bacteria break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen in the water. This can significantly lower oxygen levels in the lake, creating conditions that can suffocate fish and other aquatic species.The new project is intended to address some of these pollution sources before the water reaches the lake. According to the South Florida Water Management District, the treatment system will use aquatic vegetation within stormwater treatment cells to remove nutrients from incoming water. The district describes it as one of the largest water quality projects planned north of Lake Okeechobee.How wetlands can help clean polluted waterWetlands naturally slow down the movement of water, allowing suspended particles to settle rather than flow into rivers and lakes. Their vegetation also plays an important role in absorbing nutrients such as phosphorus, while wetland soils can retain some of these substances.In the proposed Florida project, water will pass through a series of treatment areas containing aquatic vegetation. As it moves through the system, plants, soil and other natural processes are expected to reduce the amount of phosphorus entering Lake Okeechobee.However, the project is still under development, and its environmental benefits remain projections rather than measured results. The district has not yet provided a confirmed estimate of how much phosphorus the proposed system will remove once it begins operating.The project is also expected to maintain existing flood protection for nearby communities while providing recreational opportunities in the area.The Kissimmee River's long journey towards restorationThe Kissimmee River once followed a winding, meandering course for approximately 103 miles through central Florida. Its floodplain supported extensive wetlands that provided habitats for fish, birds and other wildlife. However, following severe flooding in the 1940s, authorities began looking for ways to control the river and protect nearby communities.The US Army Corps of Engineers subsequently modified the river as part of the Central and Southern Florida Project. During the 1960s, engineers straightened and channelised the waterway by creating the C-38 canal, transforming its natural meandering course into a deep, straight channel designed to move water more quickly.While the project improved flood control, it also disrupted the river's natural floodplain. The changes reduced the seasonal flooding that sustained surrounding wetlands, affecting habitats and the wildlife that depended on them.Recognising the ecological damage, restoration efforts eventually began to reverse some of these changes. The Kissimmee River Restoration Project, authorised by Congress in 1992, involved filling sections of the artificial canal, removing levees and restoring the river's historic meandering flow.According to the South Florida Water Management District, the restoration programme aims to restore 44 miles of meandering river and nearly 20,000 acres of wetlands. It has already re-established continuous water flow along 24 miles of the restored river.The proposed 4,800-acre treatment area represents another effort to improve the health of the wider Kissimmee-Okeechobee ecosystem, this time by addressing the nutrients carried by water before they reach Lake Okeechobee.What happens next?The Lower Kissimmee Basin project has been under development since 2019, with planning, preliminary design and land acquisition taking place over the following years. In February 2026, the South Florida Water Management District purchased the project property and executed the contract.The district has also scheduled a public meeting for November 5, 2026, to present the project plan and discuss construction timelines and recreational features.While the proposed wetlands offer another approach to tackling nutrient pollution, important details are still awaited, including the expected amount of phosphorus that will be removed and when the treatment system will begin operating.For now, the project reflects a broader effort to work with natural systems to address some of the environmental problems created by decades of changing waterways and managing water primarily for human needs.

articles.title: A cupboard buried when Mount Vesuvius destroyed Pompeii in AD 79 has yielded 38 bronze coins and at least 24 tiny childhood charms; archaeologists say the objects reveal glimpses of a family's lost everyday life
articles.summary: Have you ever thought about how our ancestors lived?
articles.body: Have you ever thought about how our ancestors lived? The things that we commonly use now, like Wi-Fi, smartphones and fancy cars, did not exist even a few years ago, so what can we expect from the people who lived hundreds of years ago? The mere thought of their existence fascinates historians and archaeologists as well. To know more about them is to know humanity, to understand how we came here and who we are better. Ultimately, to know is to be. To be a better human.We often associate archaeological discoveries with grand monuments, royal tombs and ancient treasures from lost civilisations. But sometimes, it is the smallest and most ordinary objects that tell us the most about how people actually lived thousands of years ago. Civilisation was not built in palaces; it was built around communities. Everyday objects, like a perfume bottle, a cooking pot, a handful of coins or even a childhood necklace, can reveal details about the everyday lives of the masses.In a recent discovery at Pompeii, according to the Pompeii Archaeological Park, Italian archaeologists have uncovered the remains of a wooden cupboard that had remained sealed for nearly 2,000 years after Mount Vesuvius destroyed the ancient Roman city in AD 79. The cupboard, reconstructed from traces preserved in a house on Via dell'Abbondanza, one of the busiest streets of ancient Pompeii, contained a collection of household belongings, including 38 bronze coins, cosmetic utensils, cooking vessels and at least 24 tiny childhood charms. Together, these objects offer an intimate glimpse into the personal habits, work and memories of someone who lived in the city before the volcanic eruption buried it under metres of ash.What did archaeologists find inside the ancient cupboard?Among the most interesting discoveries was a necklace containing at least 24 tiny objects made from different materials, including bone, glass plate, earthenware and rock crystal. These objects included miniature representations of ancient gods such as Bes and Mercury, worshipped by the people of that era, along with small hands, feet, pine cones and a bunch of grapes.The objects are known as crepundia, a type of necklace worn by Roman children as protective amulets. Apart from their symbolic significance, the small objects could also produce sounds when they moved, acting as rattles that helped adults keep track of young children.In Roman traditions, these necklaces were not necessarily discarded once a child grew older. Some people continued to keep them into adulthood as reminders of their childhood, making the discovery particularly personal. Archaeologists cannot determine who owned the necklace, but its presence among the household belongings suggests that it may have held sentimental value for someone living in the house.The cupboard also contained several objects associated with everyday personal care and household activities. Archaeologists found a pair of tweezers, a small glass bottle that may have been used for perfume or ointment, and an incense burner. Alongside these were bronze, glass and ceramic vessels, cooking pots and other household objects.Another interesting discovery was a collection of lead weights stored in a small wooden box. These may have been used for commercial activities, suggesting that someone living in the house could have been involved in trade.38 bronze coins and objects that nobody returned to collectApart from the childhood charms and household belongings, archaeologists also discovered a small woven container holding 38 bronze coins. The container was made from plant material and had preserved the coins together for nearly two millennia.The presence of the coins alongside objects that may have carried personal and sentimental value raises an interesting question about what happened to the people who lived in the house when Mount Vesuvius erupted.According to archaeologists, the fact that both money and personal belongings remained inside the cupboard suggests that the residents may not have had enough time to retrieve them when the eruption struck.However, the exact circumstances of their departure and what happened to the household members remain unknown. Archaeologists have not been able to establish the identity of the people who owned these objects.A house that remained hidden for centuriesInterestingly, the house where these coins were found was excavated in 1912. However, archaeologists have just now decided to explore some of the rooms behind it as part of a wider restoration project.The house is located on Via dell'Abbondanza, a major street in ancient Pompeii. The discovery is a reminder of how much of Pompeii's everyday history remains buried beneath the ancient city. While the site is widely known for its preserved buildings, paintings and public spaces, household objects such as these offer another way of understanding the people who once lived there.As Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of the Pompeii Archaeological Park, explained, the discovery allows archaeologists to bring together different traces of an individual's life, including personal habits, work and memories.Nearly 2,000 years later, these seemingly ordinary objects give us a glimpse of how people actually lived in that era. Although the Roman Empire is well documented and studied as part of history, civilisations are not built in royal palaces. They are built by ordinary people and their ordinary objects, which often get lost from sight. From a child's protective necklace to a small collection of coins, the cupboard offers something that grand monuments and elaborate artworks cannot always provide: a glimpse into the personal and everyday lives of ordinary people.

articles.title: Exclusive: Here’s what 'renoa' — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Startup Everbloom's new material, renoa, is the first new fiber in 25 years, and it feels very familiar.
articles.body:
Sometimes it seems like everyone — and every occasion — demands cashmere these days.

Numerous brands sell cashmere sweaters, from Bruno Cucinelli’s $7,900 cable knit cardigan to Quince’s $50 crewneck . Menswear company Loro Piana has made cashmere a cornerstone of its lineup, helping to drive the LVMH division’s valuation above €11 billion . There are even cashmere running shirts .

But as cashmere has spread throughout the fashion industry, it’s not for everyone. It’s still relatively expensive, hard to care for, and environmental fraught. The goats that produce cashmere have been trashing rangelands across Central Asia.

That may change, though. I recently experienced an alternative fiber called renoa, developed by a startup called Everbloom , that’s washable and promises to be more affordable. It could bring the cashmere experience, via a substitute material, to more products and people.

Renoa is made from sources of waste protein, including cashmere and wool scraps as well as down and feather “lint” leftover from the bedding industry. Everbloom processes the waste into a powder and blends it with a biodegradable biopolymer, and the combination is then extruded to the right length and diameter to mimic specific natural fibers.

Renoa was recently approved as the first new fiber classification in 25 years by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which regulates fiber labeling in the U.S.

Everbloom has been developing the new fiber for three years, and is currently in the process of scaling up. The startup developed its own AI model for material science, and a cashmere substitute is the first product.

Last month, I stopped by Everbloom’s headquarters in New York City, which sits 15 floors above 5 th Avenue, kitty corner from Bryant Park. There, co-founder and CEO Sim Gulati walked me through a range of products made with its company’s cashmere-like renoa, including a crewneck sweater, a pair of knit gloves, and a scarf.

The sweater and gloves were soft and light, but the scarf was the most notable. It didn’t look like much, but it had been through the kind of hell and back that a pure cashmere scarf wouldn’t survive. It was a custom item that Everbloom had knit to test renoa, and Gulati had been wearing and washing it for months, including a trip through the tumble dryer before I saw it. It wasn’t pilled, and Gulati said it hadn’t shrunk, either.

Everbloom is currently working with a range of companies to get renoa into consumer products. The first are likely to feature renoa as a blended fiber, making up around 20% of the material in a cashmere sweater, for example. The first product is expected to hit the market in the second quarter of 2027 Gulati said.

The 80/20 cashmere-renoa blend that I felt was extremely close to the real thing, and Gulati said that additional finishing that accompanies commercial garments should eliminate any differences without compromising the washability and stability of the garment. After my visit, I kept thinking about various items in my closet that could benefit from those features. When renoa lands on shelves next year, I’ll be keeping an eye out for it.

articles.title: Florida has allocated $3 million to acquire a 642-acre property along the Suwannee River; officials say ending its current land use could save 159,000 gallons of water daily and reduce nutrient inputs
articles.summary: We all love to take a walk across the riverfronts in the evening. Both socially and ecologically, they hold great significance.
articles.body: We all love to take a walk across the riverfronts in the evening. Both socially and ecologically, they hold great significance. Rivers are among the most important natural resources for everyday use, but protecting them is not always just about cleaning the water or removing waste that has already entered the ecosystem. Sometimes it is also about protecting the nearby land, understanding how it affects the environment. From agriculture and development to excessive water consumption, human activities can gradually put pressure on rivers, springs and wildlife that depends on them.In an effort to protect one such ecosystem in Florida, the state has allocated $3 million to acquire a 642-acre property along the Suwannee River. The funding will allow the Suwannee River Water Management District to purchase the Suwannee Sandhill Tract-Drew Property in Suwannee County, which includes approximately 1.5 miles of river frontage. According to the district, ending the property's current land use could save an estimated 158,800 gallons of water every day and reduce nutrient application by around 100,000 pounds annually.The funding is part of a wider $100 million investment announced by Florida Governor Ron DeSantis for 45 projects aimed at protecting the state's water resources, restoring springs and expanding alternative water supplies.Why is Florida acquiring the 642-acre property?The property is located within the Suwannee Basin Management Action Plan area, a region covered by a restoration framework designed to address water pollution and improve the health of rivers and springs. The acquisition is expected to help reduce pressure on local water resources by allowing the district to discontinue the property's existing land use.According to the Suwannee River Water Management District, the property currently requires an estimated 158,800 gallons of water per day. Once the district acquires the land and ends its current use, that water consumption can be avoided. The project is also expected to reduce approximately 100,000 pounds of nutrient application every year, limiting the amount of nutrients that could potentially reach nearby waterways.Excess nutrients, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, can contribute to poor water quality and excessive algae growth in aquatic ecosystems, known as algal blooms. It is the phenomenon where, due to nutrient abundance, algae and cyanobacteria take over the water surface, blocking sunlight and oxygen supply for the other aquatic life. When these nutrients enter rivers and springs through runoff, they can disturb the natural balance of the ecosystem and affect the plants and animals that depend on it.The district believes that reducing water use on the property will also support the recovery of the Lower Santa Fe and Ichetucknee rivers' Minimum Flows and Minimum Water Levels. These are established thresholds intended to ensure that water withdrawals do not cause significant harm to rivers, springs and other natural resources.What will happen to the land after the acquisition?Once the property is acquired, the district plans to restore it to its natural Florida landscape. The restoration is expected to improve wildlife habitats and protect the surrounding waterways, while also creating additional opportunities for people to enjoy the area.The property will also be opened for public recreation, including seasonal hunting. This means the acquisition is not limited to reducing water consumption and nutrient application, but also aims to protect the natural landscape while allowing the public to access it.Hugh Thomas, executive director of the Suwannee River Water Management District, said that bringing the property into public ownership would help reduce water use, limit nutrient inputs and restore natural habitat. He also noted that the project would create additional opportunities for the public to enjoy this part of North Florida.Florida's wider $100 million water conservation investmentThe $3 million allocated for the Suwannee Sandhill Tract-Drew Property is part of a larger state investment announced on October 28, covering 45 projects across Florida. The funding has been divided between two programmes, with $50 million going towards springs restoration and another $50 million supporting alternative water supplies.The Springs Restoration Grant Program will support 23 projects aimed at improving water quality and spring flows. According to the governor's office, these projects are expected to reduce total nitrogen by more than 55,000 pounds annually through wastewater upgrades and other improvements.The remaining $50 million will support 22 projects intended to reduce Florida's dependence on traditional freshwater sources. These include expanding the use of reclaimed water, improving aquifer recharge and developing alternative water supplies.Together, these projects reflect the state's efforts to address both the quality and availability of freshwater. In the case of the Suwannee River property, the approach begins with the land itself. By ending its current use and allowing the landscape to recover, officials hope to reduce pressure on the river while protecting the natural habitat that surrounds it.

articles.title: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been killed by a wooden spear deliberately aimed at his heart, scientists say, offering rare evidence of targeted violence among our closest ancient relatives
articles.summary: Everybody is aware of the story of Cain and Abel, the biblical tale of the world's first murder.
articles.body: Everybody is aware of the story of Cain and Abel, the biblical tale of the world's first murder. But what if I tell you that the story of human anger and violence goes way beyond what we can imagine? Everyone hears from their grandfathers and grandmothers how good and lovely the world was before, and they too have heard the same story, almost making early humans seem like they lived in an actual heaven.Factually, long before modern civilisation, our ancestors lived in caves and depended on hunting and gathering for survival, but what if their psychology was not very different from ours? Anger, greed and a thirst for possession grasped them as much as we deal with them. That might be one of the reasons why people find their life's solutions in a book written thousands of years ago. Maybe we have not changed as much as we think. A recent discovery in Iraqi Kurdistan has offered rare evidence of what could be one of the earliest known cases of deliberate lethal violence involving a wooden spear.According to a study published in the journal Scientific Reports, researchers from the University of Cambridge have discovered a 75,000-year-old Neanderthal skeleton with a small, circular hole in its left shoulder blade. The injury suggests that a sharpened wooden spear may have passed through the individual's chest, potentially in an attack deliberately aimed at the heart. The remains, named Shanidar A, were discovered in Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan and could represent the oldest known evidence of fatal interpersonal violence involving a wooden spear in the hominin fossil record.A 15 mm hole that may reveal a deadly attackOne of the most interesting aspects of the discovery is the condition of the shoulder blade, also known as a scapula. The bone is extremely delicate, with some parts so thin that light can pass through them. Yet, it remained almost completely intact after spending around 75,000 years beneath approximately 7.5 metres of rock and sediment.The only major damage was a remarkably circular opening measuring around 15 millimetres across. According to the researchers, the shape of the hole provides an important clue about the weapon that may have caused it. Spears with flint or stone tips generally leave flatter or more angular openings, while the rounded shape of this injury is consistent with a sharpened wooden point.Based on their reconstruction, the researchers believe the spear entered the front of the individual's left chest, passed through a lung and probably major blood vessels before piercing the shoulder blade from behind. The force and position of the injury suggest that the weapon may have been deliberately directed towards the heart, causing a rapidly fatal wound.The researchers also identified small fragments of bone displaced during the impact. Their position and the bevelled edges around the opening helped the team reconstruct the direction in which the weapon travelled. The evidence suggests that the spear entered from above and moved downwards through the body.Was it a deliberate murder or a hunting accident?The question we all have been thinking about. Although the injury appears consistent with a targeted attack, researchers have not been able to establish with certainty what actually happened to Shanidar A. One possibility is that the individual was attacked by another Neanderthal, while another is that the injury was just a tragic incident during hunting.Neanderthals were another human species that coexisted with Homo sapiens and hunted large and dangerous animals, sometimes at close range using thrusting spears. An accident involving such a weapon could also have caused a fatal injury. Dr Emma Pomeroy, the lead author of the study from the University of Cambridge's Department of Archaeology, acknowledged that hunting large animals such as mammoths could have resulted in similar injuries.The other side of Neanderthal life: care and survivalInterestingly, the possible violent death of Shanidar A was not the only thing researchers discovered from his remains. His teeth showed evidence of an earlier severe facial injury, which had damaged one of his front teeth and pushed neighbouring teeth inward. However, the individual appears to have survived this injury for at least a year, possibly longer.Researchers believe that such an injury would have made eating difficult, meaning that Shanidar A may have depended on other members of his group for support. According to Dr Emma Pomeroy, surviving with such damage would likely have required some form of care from others, possibly through softer foods that were easier to eat.The discovery not only opens up our understanding of the physical aspects of Neanderthals but also their social behaviour, how the inability of one member brings care from the community. This shows the two aspects of human civilisation itself: love and care, and anger and greed, with Cain and Abel represented in a single finding.

articles.title: NASA hopes the commercial space industry can help save Hubble
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope will come crashing to Earth sometime in the 2030s without a boost.
articles.body: Gravity is a cruel mistress, slowly dragging the famed telescope ever closer to its ultimate demise with every day. Hubble is in no immediate danger of burning up in the Earth’s atmosphere, but its time will run out in the early to mid 2030s unless its orbit is boosted. So NASA is taking proposals from the private sector to see if anyone can save it. In a post on NASA’s site, Administrator Jared Isaacman said: > “Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible … If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.” The agency will keep the Request for Information open through November 30th at 3 PM ET.

articles.title: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric car batteries smaller, lighter and longer-lasting, potentially letting drivers travel farther on a single charge without carrying a heavier battery
articles.summary: Every day we look at the rise of EVs and climate concerns and think about shifting to electric vehicles.
articles.body: Every day we look at the rise of EVs and climate concerns and think about shifting to electric vehicles. But one of the biggest concerns people have when buying an electric car is its driving range. While manufacturers are constantly working to improve battery performance, making batteries larger is not always the best solution, especially when it adds more weight to the vehicle. But what if electric cars could travel farther without carrying bigger and heavier batteries? Scientists may have found a way to make this possible by rethinking how batteries are designed.Researchers from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter and longer-lasting. The team has found a way to address one of the biggest problems with anode-free batteries, a next-generation design that removes conventional materials such as graphite to make more room for energy storage. The findings were published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials.Why are scientists working on anode-free batteries?In conventional lithium-ion batteries, lithium is stored in a component called the anode, which is generally made using graphite. However, anode-free batteries work differently. Instead of using a separate anode material, lithium accumulates directly on a thin copper sheet when the battery is charged.By removing the conventional anode, manufacturers can potentially reduce the battery's weight and thickness while storing more energy in the same amount of space. This could eventually allow electric vehicles to travel longer distances without requiring larger battery packs.However, there is one major problem. During repeated charging and discharging, lithium does not always spread evenly across the copper surface. Instead, it can form sharp, needle-like structures known as dendrites. These structures can damage the battery and interfere with its performance, while an unstable protective layer around the lithium can further accelerate its deterioration.How did researchers solve the problem?To address this issue, the researchers redesigned the copper surface where lithium accumulates. Using a manufacturing technique borrowed from the semiconductor industry, known as secondary sputtering lithography, they created microscopic tube-like structures across the copper foil.Each of these tiny structures measures approximately 300 nanometres in diameter and 150 nanometres in height. Together, they increase the available surface area for lithium deposition to around four times that of an ordinary flat copper sheet. This provides more space for lithium to settle evenly instead of accumulating in concentrated areas and forming damaging spikes.The researchers also applied an extremely thin coating of MXene, a two-dimensional material, measuring approximately 10 nanometres in thickness. Rather than acting as a protective layer itself, the coating encourages the formation of a stable protective layer rich in lithium fluoride as the battery operates.This layer helps reduce unwanted chemical reactions between lithium and the electrolyte while also limiting the growth of damaging lithium structures.Could this change the future of electric cars?According to the researchers, the new approach could help overcome one of the major obstacles preventing anode-free batteries from becoming commercially viable. By improving the stability of lithium deposition without adding excess materials, the technology could help preserve the advantages of these batteries, particularly their reduced weight and size.Professor Jinwoo Lee, who led the research alongside Professor Hee-Tae Jung, said the study demonstrates how precise manufacturing techniques used in semiconductor production can create uniform sites for lithium deposition and a stable protective layer without adding excess lithium or changing the bulk electrolyte formulation.Although the findings are promising, further development and testing will be needed before the technology can be used in commercial electric vehicles. Still, the research offers a possible route towards batteries that take up less space, weigh less, and potentially allow electric cars to travel farther on a single charge.This is not only a good sign technologically but also towards a good cause for our climate. Many people who miss out on EVs because of this issue could be encouraged to make the switch, potentially giving a boost to EV sales.

articles.title: Einstein’s equations, if applied more carefully, may hold the answer to why the universe is expanding faster, without any need for mysterious dark energy, say scientists
articles.summary: For almost three decades, dark energy has been the standard explanation for why the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate.
articles.body: For almost three decades, dark energy has been the standard explanation for why the universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Now, a team of mathematicians is challenging this widely accepted theory. The mathematicians at the University of California, Davis, argue that the answer may already lie within Einstein’s own equations and that an invisible form of energy may not be needed at all. The findings are published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A. The researchers worked with the Einstein-Euler equations, which combine Einstein’s general relativity with the rules that govern how fluids move. They used these tools to test the leading framework for explaining the universe’s evolution since the Big Bang, known as the Lambda-cold dark matter model, and found a weak spot in its very foundation.Einstein’s equations may explainBlake Temple, the study’s corresponding author and a professor emeritus of mathematics at UC Davis, offered a simple comparison: a pencil balanced vertically on its tip. “All the forces are in balance when a pencil is standing on end, so it is a ‘solution’ of the equations. But it’s unstable. Any breath of air and it falls away,” Temple said in a release.According to him, the standard model behaves in a similar way. The mathematical structures at its core, known as Friedmann spacetimes, are unstable, and the standard solution is unusually fragile. Physicists tend to treat unstable solutions as unphysical. “Unstable solutions in physics and science are considered not physical. You’ll never observe them in nature,” Temple said. If the real universe drifts away from that model, the team argues, the accelerating expansion may not require a separate source of energy. The researchers say the answer is already contained in Einstein’s original theory of gravity."The instability of all Friedmann spacetimes to accelerated expansion suggests a simpler, more natural explanation for the acceleration of the universe than dark energy," he said.Early expansion linked to a shockwave?The research did not begin as a rethink of cosmology. According to Temple, the team first wondered whether a massive shockwave could explain the early expansion, with the unexpected acceleration coming from a wave trailing behind it. This very question led them to these findings. "Our first idea was that maybe the universe was expanding because there was a shockwave, and the anomalous acceleration was the expanding wave behind that shockwave. Then we realised there's a family of self-similar solutions during the radiation epoch of the Big Bang, which might model that expanding wave,” Temple said.The researchers used Einstein’s equations to examine whether the standard model of the universe remains stable when slightly disturbed. They found that these disturbances grow rather than fade away during the period when matter dominated the universe. The results are striking. They suggest that the conventional mathematical descriptions of the expanding universe are vulnerable to disturbances that grow rather than fade."We prove that, like Einstein's static model, the Friedmann spacetimes are all unstable to radial perturbation at large length scales. This appears to rule out the Lambda-cold dark matter model as a viable stable solution of the Einstein equations of general relativity, with or without dark energy,” Temple said.The researchers found that radial disturbances could cause the universe to expand differently from what the standard model predicts. "This means that the Big Bang should generically look exactly like a Friedmann spacetime near the centre of symmetry, but generically one should observe accelerations away from Friedmann far from the centre,” he explained.The researchers also raise an older idea: the Copernican principle. Named after Nicolaus Copernicus, it holds that Earth and its observers do not occupy a special position in the universe. The Copernican principle must be applied consistently when evaluating competing explanations of the universe, Temple argues."Both the Lambda-cold dark matter model and a spherically symmetric spacetime produce a special place where we must lie for the model to be physically plausible. If this principle rules out one, it has to rule out the other,” Temple said.The research was supported by the United Kingdom’s Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the American Institute of Mathematics SQuaREs Program.

articles.title: Google is building a robot doctor for NASA, as Artemis mission advances from Moon to Mars, and says it will help astronauts to handle ...
articles.summary: Google and NASA are collaborating to develop an autonomous robotic medical assistant designed to support astronauts facing health emergencies and manage
articles.body: Google and NASA are collaborating to develop an autonomous robotic medical assistant designed to support astronauts facing health emergencies and manage routine operational tasks during future deep-space expeditions. According to Google, the tie-up comes as, "NASA advances its Artemis program to send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon, build a sustained human presence there with a Moon Base, and build on their foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars."The initiative aims to address a critical hurdle for long-duration spaceflight: Providing advanced healthcare when distance renders real-time communication with Earth impossible. When not handling medical duties alongside onboard crew, the dual-purpose system is envisioned to take on routine operational workloads, including hardware maintenance, equipment transport, and inventory management.The effort convenes specialists across multiple organizations, including Google Cloud, NASA’s Human Research Program, the robotics division at Johnson Space Center, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The system builds directly upon the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant, an artificial intelligence platform Google and NASA began evaluating in 2025. That project focuses on enabling crews to independently diagnose and manage medical issues when signal delays prevent rapid consultations with terrestrial flight surgeons.“An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges, including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes,” said Jim Kelly, vice president of Google’s public sector division. Presently, the project remains in an experimental phase. Current laboratory testing is focused on validating foundational robotic manipulation and general utility tasks, with project engineers noting that fully autonomous medical intervention in microgravity remains a long-term development goal.Here's the complete post by Google's Jim KellyAs NASA advances its Artemis program to send astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon, build a sustained human presence there with a Moon Base, and build on their foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars, crew safety and Earth-independent autonomy are paramount. An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges—including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes, making real-time medical guidance for crew nearly impossible.Last year, Google Public Sector shared progress on the development of the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant (CMO-DA) - an automated Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) designed to assist astronauts with real-time medical guidance in remote and isolated environments. Today, we are building on this innovation with the development of a proof-of-concept physical, robotic system that aims to support deep space missions and could assist astronauts during NASA missions.Optimizing crew time and safetyThe future Moon Base in the lunar South Pole region of the Moon is planned to support sustained human presence. Because every minute in space is a strictly limited resource, reducing the physical burden on astronauts to maximize their time for science and discovery is a top priority. To potentially address this challenge, NASA’s Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center Robotics Team, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) collaborated with Google Public Sector to develop a robotic system. By handling routine logistics, this system could free up astronauts to focus on what humans do best: complex science and discovery.To maximize its utility for a lean crew, the robotic system is designed as a versatile "payload" handler capable of managing cargo, logistics, and equipment. When not needed for routine maintenance like organizing tools or securing compartments, it can pivot to medical support. For example, if an astronaut experiences severe back pain—a potential symptom of kidney stones—the robot could retrieve and prepare an ultrasound machine. This enables the human crew medical officer to focus entirely on analyzing the scan and treating the patient.Adapting spatial awareness and vision-language-action models for robotic systemsOperating safely alongside humans in confined spacecraft is a complex challenge. Unlike factory robots in fixed, human-free environments, space systems utilizing Super Intelligence (SI) require flexible, human-directed tools to safely adapt to close quarters. Because they must also rely on limited sensory input like cameras, JPL is adapting satellite situational awareness intelligence tools—originally designed to track objects in orbit—to help the robotic system navigate and understand its 3D surroundings.To test this safely at Johnson Space Center’s iMETRO facility, Google DeepMind’s MuJoCo simulator was used, which is an advanced physics engine that allows the SI to practice complex movements in a highly accurate virtual environment before touching real hardware. In a recent proof-of-concept technology demonstration, the robotic system was tasked with a complex "pick-and-place" maneuver to locate and move a medical bag. By implementing an "eye-to-hand" camera configuration for enhanced spatial awareness, the open-source Pi0 model—developed by Physical Intelligence on Google Cloud infrastructure— achieved an initial 85% baseline success rate in these early lab environments, providing a strong foundation for the next phase of rigorous training and safety refinement. Because vision-language-action (VLA) models connect language directly to physical movement, astronauts could direct the robotic system flexibly via standard English text prompts.Space: the ultimate edge-computing environmentProcessing these complex tasks requires significant computing power, which presents another hurdle: space is the ultimate edge computing environment. Spacecraft cannot rely on continuous connections to Earth-based data centers. To solve this, the Google team harnessed Google Cloud G4 instances to rapidly train the underlying models, fine-tuning the 4-billion parameter Pi0 model in just 2.5 hours. Crucially, they demonstrated that the fine-tuned models can then operate locally on compact, energy-efficient edge devices. Over the last two years, the team tested approximately 15 different edge computing devices to find ones that run efficiently on lightweight, low-power hardware required for future Mars missions.Pioneering the future of crew safety and space explorationLooking ahead, the ultimate goal is to build a robotic system that can execute a variety of tasks via simple voice instructions, under the astronauts’ direct supervision and command. For instance, the robot might be directed to assist with routine health monitoring—such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds—under the strict guidance of a human crew medical officer. This ensures astronauts receive the physical assistance they might not be able to perform by themselves, without ever replacing human decision-making.This collaboration between Google Public Sector and NASA can help pave the way for increasingly difficult missions that push the bounds of scientific discovery.You use AI every day. articles.title: NASA’s Chandra decodes a giant radio-wave formation shaped like a musical treble clef; a black hole’s outburst followed by a collision between galaxy clusters created it
articles.summary: Astronomers have traced the origins of an unusual cosmic formation resembling a musical treble clef to an ancient black hole eruption and a subsequent
articles.body: Astronomers have traced the origins of an unusual cosmic formation resembling a musical treble clef to an ancient black hole eruption and a subsequent collision between two galaxy clusters. According to NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, the discovery offers fresh insight into how violent events can reshape enormous structures across the universe. The formation, nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because of its distinctive appearance in radio observations, had long presented a challenge to astronomers. Its location behind the plane of the Milky Way makes it difficult to observe, as foreground stars, gas and dust obscure much of the region. By combining observations across multiple wavelengths, researchers were able to piece together a possible explanation for its unusual shape.A cosmic formation hidden behind the Milky WayThe research, led by Andrea Botteon of Italy’s National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), brought together data from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, the European Space Agency’s eROSITA telescope, the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR) radio telescope network and the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope (UKIRT).The observations revealed a vast reservoir of extremely hot gas surrounding the formation, indicating that it lies within a galaxy cluster. Further analysis showed that the region is not a single, undisturbed cluster but two clusters in the process of merging. Galaxy clusters are among the largest gravitationally bound structures in the universe. They contain hundreds of galaxies, along with immense quantities of hot gas. When two such systems collide, the resulting disturbances can generate shock waves and alter the physical conditions of the material within them.How a black hole helped shape the Treble ClefThe researchers believe the formation developed in two stages, beginning with an outburst from a supermassive black hole near the centre of the galaxy cluster. Such black holes can release enormous amounts of energy, launching jets and driving clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields into their surroundings. In this case, the eruption is thought to have produced bright radio emissions as the particles moved through space at speeds approaching that of light.Over time, the particles lost energy and the radio emission weakened. The subsequent collision between the two galaxy clusters may then have compressed the cloud or re-energised its particles, causing it to shine more brightly in radio wavelengths once again. Shock waves generated by the collision could also have contributed to this revival. The process helps explain why the radio structure has such a striking appearance despite the considerable time that may have passed since the black hole’s initial outburst.X-ray observations reveal evidence of a collisionTo investigate the merger, the team examined the distribution of hot gas using X-ray observations from Chandra. The gas appeared broadly oval-shaped, but subtle variations in its distribution offered clues about the collision. The researchers used an image-processing technique to remove the cluster’s symmetrical oval profile, making deviations from that shape easier to identify. The resulting image showed stronger X-ray emission on either side of the cluster’s centre, suggesting that the collision occurred along a roughly left-to-right direction from the perspective of the image.The scientists estimate that the direct collision took place a few hundred million years ago, with the two clusters now moving away from one another. The X-ray evidence supports the idea that the merger disturbed the surrounding gas and helped revive the radio-emitting particles responsible for the Treble Clef.When cosmic structures resemble familiar symbolsThe Treble Clef’s resemblance to musical notation is an example of pareidolia, a common perceptual phenomenon in which people recognise familiar patterns in otherwise unrelated shapes. The formation has no physical connection to music; its nickname simply reflects the distinctive outline revealed by radio observations.The combined image brings together the different layers of the discovery: X-rays show the hot gas associated with the merging clusters, radio observations reveal the treble-clef-shaped structure, and infrared data provide additional detail about the surrounding field.By connecting the radio formation to both black hole activity and a galaxy-cluster merger, the findings show how separate cosmic events can combine to produce unusual structures on enormous scales. They also demonstrate the value of observing the universe in different wavelengths, particularly in regions where foreground material makes conventional observations difficult.

articles.title: SpaceX could buy Boost Mobile as part of its big mobile carrier plans
articles.summary: SpaceX has held discussions with Boost Mobile about a potential deal that could involve acquiring the budget-friendly carrier or accessing its network, according to The Washington Post.
articles.body: SpaceX has discussed a deal with Boost Mobile to launch its own service through the budget-friendly carrier, according to a report from The Washington Post. The deal, which comes as SpaceX aims to make Starlink a “major” mobile carrier, reportedly involves the Elon Musk-owned company acquiring Boost Mobile or accessing its network. Musk discussed the potential agreement with Charlie Ergen, chairman of Boost Mobile parent company EchoStar, last month, as reported by The Washington Post. Boost Mobile’s network is currently powered by T-Mobile and AT&T, meaning SpaceX may need permission from the two carriers to launch its service. Neither SpaceX nor Boost Mobile immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment. In recent months, SpaceX has ramped up efforts to build out its mobile service, which will combine its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial network. The company acquired wireless spectrum licenses from EchoStar last year and recently purchased a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses that could allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate buildings. Last month, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks to gain access to at least 80,000 cell sites in the US.

articles.title: Northwood Space raises $375M Series C at a $2B valuation from a16z and DFJ growth | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Space infrastructure company Northwood Space on Monday said it had raised $375 million in a Series C round co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and DFJ Growth, valuing the company at $2 billion.
articles.body:
Space infrastructure company Northwood Space on Monday said it had raised $375 million in a Series C round co-led by Andreessen Horowitz and DFJ Growth, valuing the company at $2 billion.

Founded in 2022, Northwood builds antennas, software and other technologies that help satellites communicate better with Earth. Bridgit Mendler, co-founder and former actress, serves as its CEO.

The company last raised a $100 million Series B in January, also co-led by Andreessen Horowitz, along with a nearly $50 million contract with the U.S. Space Force to upgrade the nation’s “satellite control network,” TechCrunch previously reported.

This latest round also includes a financial agreement with HSBC that, along with the funding, will be used to scale the company, hire and fulfill existing contracts, the startup said.
